Article Title: Hurricane threat in Southern California: 90% chance of disturbance to turn into depression
Article Text:
This satellite image shows Hurricane Karina strengthening off the southern tip of Baja California. (Photo: NOAA via AP)

Models show possible Southern California approach

Tropical storm landfalls rare in California

Karina reaches Category 3 ahead of forecast

Marine heat wave keeps coastal waters unusually warm

El Niño has more than 90% chance of becoming very strong

A tropical disturbance in the eastern Pacific now has a 90% chance of becoming a tropical depression within 48 hours, while weather models cited by Southern California meteorologists show it could strengthen into a hurricane later this week before weakening and potentially moving towards the region.The US National Hurricane Center (NHC) said the system, designated EP95 — its identifier for the eastern Pacific disturbance being monitored, was well offshore southwestern Mexico late Sunday and moving generally northwest at 10 to 15 mph. Its showers and thunderstorms remained disorganised, but conditions favoured further development.An earlier NHC outlook had put the 48-hour formation chance at 80% and the seven-day probability at 90%, figures cited by National Weather Service (NWS) meteorologist Bryan Lewis. The centre later raised the shorter-term probability to 90%.A tropical depression has maximum sustained winds of 38 mph or less. Under official NHC classifications, a tropical storm has winds of 39 to 73 mph, while hurricane strength begins at 74 mph."Once the depression forms, the National Hurricane Center will then likely write a discussion about it and include probabilities of tropical storm or even hurricane formation, so stay tuned for that," Lewis said.The NHC has not yet issued an official track or intensity forecast for EP95, meaning projections of a hurricane and a possible Southern California approach remain model scenarios rather than an official forecast.Kaj Goldberg, a meteorologist with KTLA, a Los Angeles television station, said forecasters were closely watching the disturbance. The station said weather prediction models showed a strong possibility of an eye developing off Baja California by Thursday, although the NHC has not forecast an eye forming at this stage. "This is the disturbance that, if it does form and come together, could make its way right into Southern California about one week from today," Goldberg said.He said the system could reach hurricane strength by Friday or Saturday before weakening by Saturday night or early Sunday. Under the scenario discussed by KTLA, it could then move farther north and make landfall in Southern California as a tropical storm.The station said such a track could bring heavy rain and extreme humidity into the following week, with flooding possible.The NWS is more cautious about those potential impacts. Lewis separately told the Los Angeles Times that there was still a high degree of uncertainty over whether the developing system would bring rain to Southern California, although higher surf and stronger rip currents were more likely over the Labor Day weekend.Direct tropical-storm landfalls from the Pacific are rare in California. An unnamed storm struck near Long Beach in 1939, while Hurricane Nora entered California as a tropical storm in 1997 after first making landfall in Mexico, according to the NWS. "However, several tropical systems have weakened below tropical storm strength before making landfall," Lewis said. "Most recently, Hilary brought significant rainfall and impacts to Southern California in August 2023. Hilary was not a tropical storm by the time it reached California."The NHC's final analysis found that Hilary lost its tropical characteristics over northern Baja California and became post-tropical before moving into Southern California. Despite weakening, it brought significant rainfall and flooding to the region.The disturbance is developing during an active period in the Pacific. KTLA reported that three storms were contributing to increased swells in Southern California, including Hurricane Karina, which was then a Category 1 storm and was forecast to potentially reach Category 3 by late Monday night or early Tuesday.Karina strengthened much faster. By Sunday evening it had become a Category 3 major hurricane with sustained winds of 125 mph while remaining far offshore and moving westwards. No coastal watches or warnings were in effect, though the NHC said its swells would generate dangerous surf and rip currents along southwestern Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula.The NWS separately warned of a high rip-current risk along Los Angeles County beaches. An earlier Sunday forecast listed surf of up to 6 feet and water temperatures as high as 76 degrees Fahrenheit, while a later update listed temperatures of 71 to 75 degrees.KTLA linked the potential storm to a "super" El Niño brewing in the Pacific and noted that the climate pattern is associated with warmer waters in the eastern Pacific.Citing NWS data, it reported sea surface temperatures across Southern California at 5 to 10 degrees above normal for the time of year, with readings of 74 to 76 degrees along Los Angeles County beaches.The relationship between El Niño and the current marine heat wave is more nuanced, however. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has tracked a marine heat wave off central and Southern California since May 2025, before the present El Niño developed. NOAA says more recent warming off Southern California may increasingly reflect El Niño's influence.El Niño is characterised by unusually warm waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific and can affect atmospheric circulation and tropical-cyclone activity.The Climate Prediction Center, part of the National Weather Service, says El Niño is strengthening and has a greater than 90% chance of becoming a "very strong event" during the Northern Hemisphere fall and winter of 2026-27.The climate pattern can influence conditions in which tropical cyclones develop, but it does not determine the path or strength of an individual storm.For EP95, the next significant development will be the start of NHC advisories if the disturbance becomes sufficiently organised. Those would provide official track and intensity forecasts and indicate whether the modelled Southern California scenario gains or loses support.
Article Summary: Tropical disturbance in the eastern Pacific now has a 90% chance of becoming a tropical depression within 48 hours. Weather models cited by Southern California meteorologists show it could strengthen into a hurricane later this week. Direct tropical-storm landfalls from the Pacific are rare in California.

Article Title: A man who grew up poor and fatherless and barely finished high school went on to open 54 Burger King restaurants across three US states; his foundation has since donated more than $2 million
Article Text:
Gullo got his start as a night manager at Burger King. Over the years he built up his business interests and eventually established a franchise empire in three states.

From success to philanthropy

A memoir built on life lessons

From heart surgery to pickleball pioneer

Gullo’s influence goes beyond business and philanthropy. In 2008, he had quintuple bypass surgery and then developed heart failure. He learned pickleball. The sport helped him lose 100 pounds and inspired him to grow pickleball in Northern Utah.

Service that connects people

An American dream to give

John Gullo’s story of overcoming a poor, fatherless childhood in a rough Italian neighborhood of Buffalo, New York to becoming a successful businessman and philanthropist is a true American success story. According to a Fox Business report, Gullo, now 82, built a career around Burger King, eventually opening 54 restaurants in Utah, Arizona and Wisconsin. His accomplishments included opening what is thought to be the first Burger King attached to a gas station, in Hurricane, Utah.But Gullo’s definition of success has never been about money. He grew up with very little and developed a belief that happiness, service and generosity were more meaningful than wealth. The report states that Gullo got his start as a night manager at Burger King. Over the years he built up his business interests and eventually established a franchise empire in three states. Later, he sold his restaurants, finding he missed working directly with young people and being involved in their development. The next chapter of his life soon focused on his passion for mentoring kids and giving back, adds the Fox Business report.In 2002, Gullo founded the American Dream Foundation, using his business success to benefit charitable causes. For the last 25 years, the foundation has donated more than $2 million to organizations and projects serving children, families, classrooms, firefighters and people with disabilities. Gullo has supported causes such as Prevent Child Abuse, the Children’s Justice Center, Enable Industries, the American Fallen Fire Memorial, Youth in Transition, the Ogden Police Department’s Let’s Play Program and the Treehouse Children’s Museum. The foundation also has helped fund the American Freedom Trail, which gives fifth-graders in Weber County, Utah, a chance to learn about American history and freedom.Gullo has documented his incredible story in his memoir, Extraordinary Adventures of an Ordinary Man, co-written with author, Bridget Cook-Burch. The book is a mingling of his life story with lessons to inspire young readers. Gullo has stressed the importance of learning from mistakes, taking action and seeing the opportunities life presents. All proceeds from the book are donated to charity, continuing Gullo’s long-standing commitment to giving back.Gullo’s influence goes beyond business and philanthropy. In 2008, he had quintuple bypass surgery and then developed heart failure. He learned pickleball. The sport helped him lose 100 pounds and inspired him to grow pickleball in Northern Utah. He helped build hundreds of courts, founded the Professional Pickleball Federation, and created the Tournament of Champions, including prize money he paid out of his own pocket. His work in the sport earned him a spot in the Pickleball Hall of Fame in 2024 and the Father of Professional Pickleball award.Gullo also has been working with former NBA player Thurl Bailey on charity initiatives over the past 20 years. Their friendship, despite their contrasting backgrounds and differing opinions, is symbolic of Gullo’s larger work to bring people and organizations together through service and community. He credits the Jaycees, a civic and leadership organization for young adults, with helping him overcome his introverted nature and teaching him valuable lessons on leadership, teamwork and community service.From poverty and a high school diploma barely attained, to building 54 restaurants, supporting numerous charities and helping transform pickleball, Gullo's life is proof of a belief that success is measured by more than financial achievement. Ultimately his story is about how one person can create opportunity for others. Having experienced poverty himself, Gullo has spent decades ensuring that children, families and communities have the support and opportunities he didn’t have. The American dream, to Gullo, was never just about making money. It was about building himself up and then using what he built to help others.
Article Summary: John Gullo grew up in a rough Italian neighborhood in Buffalo, New York. He built a career around Burger King, eventually opening 54 restaurants in Utah, Arizona and Wisconsin. In 2008, he had quintuple bypass surgery and then developed heart failure. The sport helped him lose 100 pounds and inspired him to grow pickleball in Northern Utah. In 2002, he founded the American Dream Foundation, using his business success to benefit charitable causes.

Article Title: In 2014, an American town was known as the 'food desert', but one man turned a college football field into a farm that generates 60,000 pounds of produce
Article Text:
A pipe dream

A resounding success

It has produced more than 50 varieties of vegetables totalling more than 30,000 pounds of produce.

Partnerships and future

Eight miles south of downtown Dallas, there lies an area that is federally recognised as a food desert, meaning there are no grocery stores or restaurants where fresh, nutritious food can be obtained for those devoid of the luxury of cars. This 95% minority, poverty-stricken area surrounds the rolling 146 acres of Paul Quinn College, a private, faith-based liberal arts college.Set in a valley on the northeast corner of campus, the field is everything you might expect at a tiny NAIA school. Bright white goalposts. A fading, antiquated scoreboard. A yellow and purple shack where fans can purchase tickets. And, tucked behind one end zone, a pair of navy blue blocking sledges for training. But there is no football practice happening on this ground, no whistles, no tackling drills and no sprints. All because no team calls this place home. Instead, the 20-yard line is occupied by bulging sweet potatoes, radishes, hens laying eggs and fresh tilapia swimming in a state-of-the-art aquaponics system, according to a report by ESPN.It was in 2007, that college President Michael Sorrell, a former college basketball player, decided to kill Paul Quinn's cash-strapped football program.Two years later, he transformed the old field into an organic farm. Yes, people said he was insane and his plan would fail, but 19 years on, the farm continues to produce."You know the Apple commercial 'Here's to the crazy ones?'" Sorrell said to the outlet back in 2014. "Well, that's us. We're proud to be the crazy ones. We weren't supposed to make it. No one thought this would work. But here we are. And I'm telling you, we think -- no, we know -- this is only the beginning. We are going to change the world with this farm."When Sorrell took the job at the college in fall 2007, it was in a financial crisis with a 1% graduation rate. He had no experience running a college, and had previously worked as a lawyer and White House special assistant. But he soon realised the healthy food scarcity the surrounding area faced. By spring, he had gained 15 pounds, thanks to lunch and dinner options that were limited to chicken shacks, convenience stores and fast food. The healthiest choice was Subway, three miles down the road.He was determined to make change and began talking with community leaders in the hope of getting a grocery store on or near campus. No one was interested, even when he offered free land. The words of his final prospective owner left a scathing mark. "He said to a friend of mine that the people in this neighbourhood don't look like his clients," Sorrell said. "And I just got furious at the injustice of it all. In the back of my mind, I may have thought that. But to hear someone say it, to have someone tell you that, basically, poor, black and brown people don't deserve what you provide? I was livid."That's when he had the idea to turn the field into a farm. He scrapped the football program, saving the university $600,000 a year. When the alumni of the program protested, he challenged them to raise $2 million to save football and none raised a dime.At a luncheon with a local entrepreneur who had been interested in community gardens, Sorrell suggested investing in the idea of farming on the field. The man said yes. Sorrell went to his board, insisting he had found the idea that was going to save the cash-strapped school, which had lost its accreditation a year earlier amid financial and academic concerns. "They said, 'It's going to make that much money?'" Sorrell recalled. "I said, 'No, it's going to serve notice as to who we are going to be. A voice for those without voices and hope for the hopeless. And if no one else wants to stand up for what's right, we will."He asked one of his employees, Elizabeth Wattley, to run the farm with absolutely no experience but an open mind. "I started reading books and Googling," Wattley said.Slowly but strongly, the farm succeeded. Through fundraising and a partnership with PepsiCo and its Food for Good initiative, a few training beds turned into the entire field. Students worked on the field as part of a work-study program that decreased their tuition. The farm became a cornerstone of the school's required social entrepreneurship program, which teaches students to become leaders and generate wealth through breaking the cycle of poverty and giving back to the community. And at minimum, 10 per cent of the farm's yield went back to the community it called home.Chanson Goodson, a member of the community, had grown up seeing posters of the football team around town but had never seen a game. Instead, when he roamed around, he would see children covered in dirt and wonder what they were doing. That is, until he became a student at Paul Quinn and took a work-study job at the farm for $10 an hour. "It was a job," he said. "Just a regular job. I would just go there and try to knock it out. I didn't want to touch dirt. I didn't want no bugs. If it was too cold, I didn't want to work. If it was too hot, I didn't want to work. It was a paycheck."But eventually, something happened. Goodson started planting vegetables, watering them, taking care of them and watching them grow. He started to show up for work early. Leave late. And take pride in the planting he had done. He pushed others to do the same. "I became absorbed in it," he said. "It became more of a responsibility than a job."Every semester, the faculty sees the same transition. The kids who don't want to be there and those who succeed. Soon, it transforms into a competition. "They're taking potatoes in the dorm. I've heard students in the dorm defending their tomatoes," Wattley said at the time.Sorrell believes it all comes back to a simple premise: the human desire to achieve. "When you are used to losing, winning seems a million miles away," he said. "What the farm does is, when you plant something, it grows. It's a simple and tangible example of your success. And you can't beat that."Since its creation in March 2010, the farm has been renamed the "WE Over Me" farm. It has produced more than 50 varieties of vegetables totalling more than 30,000 pounds of produce. It now includes a chicken coop, four active beehives and a greenhouse that houses an aquaponics system to raise tilapia. The farm sells directly to local restaurants and grocery stores as well as at farmers' markets. The farm's success has helped Paul Quinn restore its accreditation and build new partnerships with Yale, Duke and the University of Pennsylvania. The school has been named an HBCU of the Year. And Sorrell was named the HBCU President of the Year.In 2011, Wattley was watching the annual Dallas Cowboys Thanksgiving Day game when she nearly lost her mind. During a break in the action, cameras showed owner Jerry Jones looking down from his private suite as his Cowboys were beating the Miami Dolphins. He was nibbling on a radish. "That was our radish," Wattley said. "I'm sure that was the radish we harvested."Four years earlier, George Wasai, a football player in the 1980s at Bishop College, which used to occupy the campus where Paul Quinn is now, was among those fighting to keep the PQC football program alive. But when Sorrell turned the field into a farm, Wasai had an idea. He was the food and beverage director for the hospitality division of Legends, at the old Texas Stadium and at the newly constructed AT&T Stadium. Wasai mentioned the farm to one of his executive chefs, and a partnership was established.Now, an entire section of the farm is dedicated to the Cowboys. The team is Paul Quinn's largest client. Each year, Koski and Legends chefs work together to determine what high-value crops the stadium could use that will also help maximise the farm's revenue.According to a 2022 Penn University report, more than 60,000 pounds of produce are used in the dining halls and sold to local restaurants and grocery stores.The spirit of the game has not completely vanished from the field. The scoreboard with chipping paint still stands, the sledges are swallowed in bees and the light stands stand a bit crooked, all a reminder of what made way for what once was.
Article Summary: Former college basketball player Michael Sorrell decided to kill Paul Quinn's football program. Two years later, he transformed the old field into an organic farm. The farm has produced more than 50 varieties of vegetables totalling more than 30,000 pounds of produce.

Article Title: Hungry bears are entering homes, shops and neighbourhoods across the US; here’s what is driving the alarming trend
Article Text:
A severe drought is leaving bears hungry

From forests to kitchens and shops

More bears are also living near people

The encounters can turn deadly

Why the problem could get worse

A hungry pair of young black bears recently wandered into a home in Granby, Colorado, startling a resident who found them standing in his hallway. The animals eventually bolted through the front door, but the unusual intrusion is part of a much larger pattern unfolding across the American West. Reuters reported that bear sightings and conflicts are rising sharply as severe drought leaves wild animals struggling to find food. Bears have been spotted in increasingly unlikely places, from homes and shops to school areas and busy neighbourhoods. In Colorado alone, wildlife officials have recorded more than 7,000 bear sightings in 2026, already surpassing the state’s previous full-year record of about 5,400 sightings in 2019.At the heart of the problem is an unusually dry year across the western US. The region experienced an exceptionally dry winter, followed by drought conditions that have reduced the availability of plants, grasses, berries and nuts, foods that make up roughly 90% of a bear’s natural diet, according to experts and state wildlife agencies cited by Reuters.That shortage is forcing bears to travel farther and take greater risks in their search for calories.And once they reach human settlements, they can find an irresistible alternative: garbage, pet food, bird seed, fruit trees and other easily accessible sources of food. Bears have an exceptionally strong sense of smell, making residential areas particularly attractive when natural food is scarce.The consequences are increasingly visible. In Granby, bears were spotted not only inside a home but also in a vape shop. In Santa Fe, New Mexico, a bear was seen near a school, while another climbed a tree close to a farmers market in Denver. A bear cub also recently wandered into a restaurant in Aspen.Colorado Parks and Wildlife received 6,129 reports of bear sightings and conflicts between January 1 and August 13, almost double the 3,115 reports recorded during the same period last year. The agency has also reported a significant increase in property damage linked to bears searching for food. The problem isn’t limited to Colorado. Wildlife authorities have reported increasing conflicts in states including New Mexico, Utah, Montana and California.Drought is only one part of the story. Decades of development have pushed homes and communities into areas that were once bear habitat. At the same time, conservation efforts have helped bear populations recover in several parts of the US.Colorado is now home to an estimated 17,000 to 20,000 black bears, according to state authorities. The state’s human population has also more than doubled over the past 50 years, increasing the amount of overlap between people and bears. This means bears are not necessarily moving into entirely unfamiliar territory. In many cases, human settlements have expanded into landscapes the animals historically used to forage.Most bear encounters do not result in attacks, and experts stress that bears generally avoid humans. But when animals become accustomed to finding food around people, the risk of conflict increases.The number of bears dying as a result of these encounters is also climbing. New Mexico authorities have killed 187 bears this year, the state’s highest number since 2011, while Utah has euthanised 39 bears, already a record for a full year. In Montana, 24 grizzlies have died this year, mostly after conflicts involving livestock or people or after being hit by vehicles.New Mexico also recorded its first fatal bear attack in 25 years this month, while a man was killed by a grizzly in Montana’s Glacier National Park in May. Fatal bear attacks, however, remain rare across the western US.Wildlife experts are particularly concerned about the coming months. Bears normally need to consume large amounts of food before winter to build up fat reserves for hibernation. With natural food supplies already depleted, they could become even more dependent on human settlements.Experts also warn that prolonged drought and warmer winters could eventually alter traditional hibernation patterns and make bears increasingly accustomed to human food. For residents, wildlife officials recommend keeping garbage secured in bear-resistant containers, bringing bins out only on collection days, removing bird feeders and keeping pet food and barbecue grills away from bears.The message from wildlife experts is simple: don’t feed a hungry bear, even if you think you’re helping. Once a bear learns that humans are a reliable source of food, it may keep returning, even after conditions in the wild improve.
Article Summary: Severe drought in the western US is leaving bears hungry and searching for food. Bears have been spotted in increasingly unlikely places, from homes and shops to school areas and busy neighbourhoods. In Colorado alone, wildlife officials have recorded more than 7,000 bear sightings in 2026. The number of bears dying as a result of these encounters is also climbing.

Article Title: UAE, Egypt coordinate over Banque Misr bank after US Treasury notice on Iran links, dollar curbs
Article Text:
Egypt's Banque Misr is reviewing US sanctions targeting its UAE branches for alleged Iran dealings

The United Arab Emirates and Egyptian central banks are coordinating over Banque Misr after the US Treasury proposed cutting off the Egyptian bank’s UAE branches from dollar transactions over alleged financial links to Iran.In a joint statement on Sunday, the two central banks said Banque Misr would take “all necessary measures” to continue its business as usual, reported Reuters.The proposed US measure is expected to take effect less than 30 days after a public comment period. It applies only to Banque Misr’s UAE branches and would prevent them from carrying out transactions in US dollars through the US financial system.Banque Misr said on Saturday that it was reviewing the US Treasury notice.The move comes as Washington steps up pressure on banks and financial institutions seen as facilitating Iran’s access to the global financial system.Meanwhile, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent told Reuters on Sunday that the department was likely to announce new secondary sanctions against Iran-linked entities every week, with banks an initial focus.“You're going to see a lot more of these every week,” Bessent said, warning banks that “it’s not okay to have Iranian money and to aid the regime.”“There can be no leakage,” Bessent added, “You're either with us or you're with the Iranians.”The Treasury launched the campaign, dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast”, last week, saying it aims to cut off the financial networks that help Iran generate revenue, evade sanctions and fund its activities.This came as the US treasury alleged on Friday that Banque Misr UAE had processed about $1.8 billion for 103 companies potentially linked to Iranian shadow-banking networks between January 2024 and June 2026.The Treasury described the UAE operation as a “critical node” in Iran’s access to US dollars and said some of the bank’s customers included apparent front companies used by Iran’s Ministry of Defence and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to evade sanctions.The proposed rule would prohibit US financial institutions from maintaining correspondent accounts for Banque Misr UAE and require them to take steps to prevent transactions involving the UAE bank from being processed through the US financial system.The Treasury stressed that the proposed measure applies only to Banque Misr UAE and not to the bank’s operations in other countries.Bessent said the next stage of the campaign could involve cutting institutions off entirely from the dollar-based financial system, while urging G20 finance ministers and central bank governors to sever economic ties with Iran or risk secondary sanctions.The US has also imposed sanctions on Reza Mohammad Taeedi, manager of Bank Melli’s Dubai branch, and a Hong Kong-based company accused of helping sanctioned Iranian entities access the international financial system.
Article Summary: Egypt's Banque Misr is reviewing US sanctions targeting its UAE branches for alleged Iran dealings. The US Treasury proposed cutting off the Egyptian bank’s UAE branches from dollar transactions over alleged financial links to Iran. The proposed US measure is expected to take effect less than 30 days after a public comment period.

Article Title: In 2025, Texas engineers mixed 4.5 tons of recycled plastic into a highway, replacing part of the bitumen to test how it handles extreme heat
Article Text:
Representative Image of plastic waste being transformed into road-building material for sustainable infrastructure (AI-generated image)

How researchers turn discarded plastic into road material

Why Texas is testing plastic in highways

What the Rockwall road could mean for future projects

On State Highway 205 in Rockwall, a suburb east of Dallas, engineers paved a 3,500-foot stretch of road using about 4.5 tons of recycled plastic mixed directly into the asphalt. The project, led by Sahadat Hossain, a civil engineering professor at the University of Texas at Arlington, replaces a portion of the petroleum-based bitumen that normally binds asphalt with melted plastic made from discarded bags, bottles and other everyday waste. After years of laboratory testing and smaller pavement trials, the May 2025 project brought the technology onto an active Texas highway. The team is now watching how the material performs under regular traffic, heavy vehicles and Texas heat. The idea is relatively simple: instead of sending difficult-to-recycle plastic to landfills or letting it escape into the environment, researchers want to give some of it another use while also reducing the amount of conventional petroleum-based binder needed to build roads.The technology developed by Hossain's team is designed to change the composition of asphalt without requiring an entirely different type of road. Conventional asphalt is made from aggregates such as crushed stone and sand held together by bitumen, a sticky petroleum-based binder. In the Texas project, roughly 8% to 10% of the bitumen is replaced with recycled plastic. The plastic waste is first cleaned and shredded into small pieces before being introduced into the hot asphalt mixture.At high temperatures, the plastic melts and becomes incorporated into the material as the asphalt is produced. The approach is aimed at two problems at once. Plastic waste is notoriously difficult to manage, particularly when it comes from thin bags and other products that are not easily processed through standard recycling systems. At the same time, road engineers are constantly looking for ways to make asphalt last longer and withstand increasingly demanding conditions. Texas provides a particularly useful testing ground because pavement is exposed to intense summer heat as well as heavy traffic. When conventional bitumen becomes softer under high temperatures, roads can become more vulnerable to deformation, including the grooves and depressions known as rutting.Hossain's team had already spent years testing plastic-infused asphalt before taking the material onto State Highway 205. Laboratory experiments allowed researchers to examine the physical properties of different mixtures under controlled conditions, while smaller pavement trials provided an opportunity to see how the material behaved outside the lab. The Rockwall project represents a much more significant test because the road is being used normally rather than being reserved for research. Cars and trucks are passing over the material every day, while the pavement is exposed to the full range of weather conditions. That real-world exposure is important because a road can perform well in a controlled experiment and still behave differently once it is subjected to years of traffic, temperature changes and moisture. Researchers can now monitor the Rockwall section for cracking, rutting and other forms of deterioration. The results should provide a clearer picture of whether recycled plastic can remain stable inside asphalt over a long period and whether the material offers any practical advantage over conventional road construction.The project comes at a time when plastic waste has become a global environmental problem. More than 400 million tons of plastic are produced around the world each year, but less than 10% is recycled. The remainder can end up in landfills, be incinerated or enter rivers, oceans and other parts of the environment. While recycling rates vary considerably depending on the type of plastic and the country where it is collected, many everyday plastic products have limited value in existing recycling systems. That is part of the reason researchers are interested in finding uses that do not depend entirely on traditional recycling. Instead of turning waste plastic back into another plastic product, the Texas approach incorporates it into infrastructure that could remain in service for years. A road therefore becomes a potential long-term destination for material that might otherwise have been thrown away. There is also a practical reason for looking at plastic as part of asphalt. Bitumen itself is derived from petroleum, and asphalt production and road construction require large quantities of it. Replacing even a relatively small portion of the binder with another material could reduce the amount of bitumen required for a road, although the environmental and economic benefits depend on how the plastic is sourced, processed and incorporated.The researchers are not presenting the technology as a complete answer to either plastic pollution or road deterioration. Instead, the Rockwall project is testing whether the two problems can be addressed together. If the modified asphalt performs well over time, it could create another outlet for certain types of waste plastic while giving transportation agencies another material option for pavement construction. There are still questions to answer. A road has to remain safe and structurally sound for years, and any new material used at highway scale has to meet demanding engineering requirements. Researchers also need to understand how the plastic behaves as the pavement ages and whether there are any environmental concerns associated with its long-term use. Those questions cannot be answered by a single paving project, which is why continued monitoring will be central to the research.The 3,500-foot section of State Highway 205 is therefore best understood as a large-scale field experiment. The UTA team can now observe how its recycled-plastic asphalt responds to the conditions that matter most to transportation agencies: traffic, heat, weather and time. The road's performance will help researchers determine whether the laboratory results translate into a material that can be used reliably on public highways. The team has also discussed extending the work to other parts of Texas, including Fort Worth and Amarillo. Testing the material in different locations could be particularly useful because pavement conditions are not identical across the state. Traffic volumes, temperatures, weather patterns and soil conditions can all affect how a road ages. Comparing different sites would allow researchers to see whether the material's performance remains consistent outside Rockwall.For Hossain, the broader appeal of the technology lies in giving waste plastic a purpose beyond its short original lifespan. A plastic bag or bottle may be used for only minutes or days, but once incorporated into road infrastructure, the material could remain part of a working pavement for years. That does not eliminate the need to reduce plastic production, improve recycling or prevent waste from reaching the environment, but it does offer another possible route for dealing with some of the plastic that is already being discarded.
Article Summary: Texas engineers paved a 3,500-foot stretch of road using about 4.5 tons of recycled plastic mixed directly into the asphalt. The plastic waste is first cleaned and shredded into small pieces before being introduced into the hot asphalt mixture. At high temperatures, the plastic melts and becomes incorporated into the material as the asphalt is produced.

Article Title: In 1985, CNN founder Ted Turner bought thousands of acres in Florida; the former plantation became a major private wildlife landscape
Article Text:
Ted Turner. Image Credit: Architectural Digest

Why did Ted Turner buy Avalon in Florida

Importance of wildlife at Avalon

Ted owned several ranches, one of which is Avalon in Florida. Situated just outside of Tallahassee, it spans more than 20,000 acres. Image Credit: WCTV

How is Avalon managed today

Ted Turner’s Florida home

Turner’s Florida home in 2004. Image Credit: Architectural Digest

Where did Ted Turner live later in his life

Avalon as one of Ted Turner’s lasting legacy

Ted Turner’s homes were never simply places to live. The CNN founder built a remarkable property portfolio that stretched across vast ranches, wildlife landscapes and historic plantations covering roughly 2 million acres. Among the most interesting was ‘Avalon,’ a former cotton plantation near Tallahassee, Florida, that Turner bought in 1985 and gradually expanded into a much larger private landscape. Architectural Digest reported that the property had grown to about 25,000 acres by 2004, with a grand Colonial Revival house, gardens and lakes at its centre. Decades later, Avalon remains closely linked to Turner’s conservation vision. Tall Timbers reports how the estate was being managed with an eye on wildlife, habitat and its long-term future, revealing how Turner’s enormous land holdings became about more than ownership and careful stewardship of natural landscape.Turner purchased Avalon near Tallahassee in 1985. At the time, the property covered about 8,000 acres and had previously been a cotton plantation and wild quail hunting site. The name Avalon came from the legends surrounding King Arthur.As Architectural Digest reported, Turner initially considered calling it Camelot, but eventually chose Avalon because he felt it better suited what he considered a mystical place. The initial purchase was already substantial, but Turner did not stop there. By 2004, he had acquired surrounding land and increased the size of Avalon by another 25,000 acres. Turner explained that he bought more land because he wanted it and believed land was something that lasted. That expansion transformed Avalon from a large private property into a vast landscape where wildlife and land management became central to its identity.Avalon has a long history as a quail hunting property, but its role extends well beyond recreation. The property is home to quail, turkey, deer and black bears. It also supports red-cockaded woodpeckers, a declining species that has established 18 active clusters on the property, according to Tall Timbers. Land conservation has also become a major part of Avalon’s future. More than 8,000 acres were placed under a conservation easement with The Nature Conservancy in 1988. In 2023, another 13,000-plus acres were placed into conservation through Florida Forever. These agreements prevent the land from being developed. Avalon was also being considered as a long-term home for gopher tortoises relocated from areas facing development. Tall Timbers reported that more than 5,000 acres could provide suitable soil and habitat for them.The story of Avalon did not end with Turner’s purchase. Tall Timbers reports a new approach to managing the property under Karl Halbig, who arrived as its manager in August 2022. Halbig oversees more than 21,450 acres and initially resisted making immediate changes. Instead, he spent his first year learning how Avalon worked through different seasons and understanding how its various teams operated. As per Tall Timbers, he mapped the entire property using GPS, including roads, quail courses, food plots, feed trails and fields used by young birds. That information helped form a detailed management plan, giving the team a clearer way to measure whether changes were actually improving the land.At the heart of Avalon stood a 15,000-square-foot Colonial Revival house built in 1938, the same year Turner was born. The property also included gardens and several lakes, giving the home a distinctly different character from the enormous western ranches associated with Turner. Turner and actor Jane Fonda were married at Avalon in 1991. The couple later divorced in 2001, but the Florida property remained part of Turner’s wider land portfolio. As per Architectural Digest, he did not have a swimming pool at Avalon or at any of his other homes because he was simply not interested in pools. The detail offers a glimpse into the practical attitude that the surrounding land mattered more than conventional luxury features.Ted Turner became one of America’s most prominent media figures, owning an extraordinary collection of properties across the United States and Argentina. According to Architectural Digest, his land holdings eventually reached across ranches in states including Montana, New Mexico, Nebraska, Colorado, Kansas and South Dakota, as well as properties in Argentina. His homes varied considerably. Some were working ranches, while others were historic estates or wildlife-focused properties. In his later years, Turner lived on one of his Montana ranches, where fishing remained one of his favourite activities. Yet Avalon in Florida stands out because of how dramatically Turner expanded it after buying the property.Turner’s property empire was enormous, but Avalon illustrates why simply describing him as a major landowner misses part of the story. Across his ranches and estates, Turner increasingly connected land ownership with wildlife and conservation. At Avalon, that approach continues through careful habitat management, conservation agreements and efforts to protect species. Halbig described Avalon as deeply sentimental to Turner and saying that he wanted to protect the property for him. His goal was to leave the land in better condition for future generations. What began in 1985 with the purchase of an 8,000-acre former plantation grew into a landscape of more than 21,000 acres under active management. For Turner, the value of the property was not limited to the house at its centre. It was the land itself, and the wildlife and natural systems that depended on it.
Article Summary: Ted Turner owned several ranches, one of which is Avalon in Florida. Situated just outside of Tallahassee, it spans more than 20,000 acres. Avalon has a long history as a quail hunting property, but its role extends well beyond recreation. The property is home to quail, turkey, deer and black bears. Land conservation has also become a major part of Avalon’s future.

Article Title: US mayor Joe Anderson dies mysteriously at 45 after sudden collapse on Colorado hike
Article Text:
Colorado politician Joe Anderson suddenly collapsed on Colorado hike and died shortly thereafter. (Photo: Instagram @nypost)

From homelessness work to Englewood council

Anderson pushed stormwater overhaul after deadly floods

‘Always there to lend a hand’: City leaders remember Anderson

Englewood Mayor Pro Tem Joe Anderson lost his consciousness and was not breathing while hiking on the lower slopes of Quandary Peak in Summit County, according to local authorities. Sheriff's deputies were called at about 6.40am after other hikers had already begun CPR.Deputies and medical personnel continued attempts to revive him, but Anderson died at the scene. The cause of death has not been announced and is expected to be determined by the coroner, the Daily Mail reported, citing local authorities. The City of Englewood confirmed his death later on Friday.Anderson entered the Englewood City Council in November 2019 as the representative for District 3 and won another four-year term in November 2023. His council colleagues elected him mayor pro tem in December that year, and his term was scheduled to expire in November 2027.He served in pastoral roles at local churches and helped found Change the Trend, a coalition working on homelessness. The city said his work with the coalition preceded the creation of the Tri-Cities Homelessness Policy Committee, which coordinates policy across Englewood, Littleton and Sheridan.He also spent years coordinating Be a Tool, later renamed the Neighborhood Rehab Project, which organised home repairs for seniors and people with disabilities. He later represented Englewood on the Tri-Cities committee, which worked on regional homelessness services including a navigation centre and a Bridge House employment programme.Anderson was also involved in Englewood's CodeNext overhaul of development rules, backing measures that made it easier to build smaller homes as part of efforts to improve housing affordability.After deadly flooding hit Englewood in 2018, Anderson pressed the city to plan beyond immediate repairs. His position was that Englewood needed a long-term upgrade of its stormwater system without imposing costs that households and businesses could not absorb.The city later completed the $23 million South Englewood Flood Reduction Project, which added detention ponds and upgraded stormwater pipes.Mayor Othoniel Sierra described Anderson as someone who was “always there to lend a hand” as a friend, neighbour, pastor and elected official. “This is a tremendous loss for our city and our heart goes out to his family and friends during this time of loss,” he said.Outgoing City Manager Shawn Lewis called Anderson “one of the most effective, productive and positive council members I've ever worked with,” and recalled that Anderson had offered to pray for him when his parents were hospitalised during the Covid pandemic.A fundraiser has since been organised for Anderson's wife, Rebecca, and their children. Its organisers described him as a father, husband, friend and neighbour and said memorial details would be announced later.Anderson's District 3 term was due to run until November 2027. Under Englewood's charter, the remaining council members have 30 days to fill the vacancy with a 75% vote. If they fail to do so, the seat moves into the electoral process.
Article Summary: Mayor Pro Tem Joe Anderson lost consciousness and was not breathing. He was hiking on the lower slopes of Quandary Peak in Summit County, Colorado. Sheriff's deputies were called at about 6.40am after other hikers had already begun CPR. Anderson died at the scene; cause of death has not been announced.

Article Title: Maine buried 20,000 discarded tyres beneath a road to fight frost and spring mud, while turning a growing waste problem into an engineering solution
Article Text:
Maine tested old tyres beneath roads to make them stronger in spring

20,000 tyres went beneath one Maine road for a winter test

Why shredded tyres worked differently from ordinary gravel

Engineers began testing tyre chips beyond road construction

Maine had millions of old tyres with few places to go

The next test moved closer to a normal highway

Along a quiet stretch of road in Maine, engineers buried something most people would expect to see in a scrapyard rather than beneath their tyres: about 20,000 discarded car tyres. The unusual experiment was designed to tackle two problems at once. Maine’s roads face a difficult seasonal cycle, with winter freezing the ground and spring thaw turning it soft and unstable. Gravel roads can quickly develop ruts and potholes as vehicles pass over the weakened surface. At the same time, the state produces more than a million unwanted tyres each year, creating a growing waste problem with few easy outlets.University of Maine engineer Dana Humphrey wondered whether shredded tyres could become part of the solution. Cut into large chips and placed beneath a conventional gravel surface, the rubber acted differently from ordinary road fill. When spring arrived, the experimental section showed noticeably less frost penetration and deterioration than nearby parts of the road.Maine has a particularly large network of unpaved roads, many of them exposed to repeated cycles of freezing in winter and thawing in spring.As temperatures rise, water held in the ground can turn road surfaces soft. Heavy vehicles then make matters worse, leaving sections of gravel roads difficult to travel.The tyre-chip idea was developed by University of Maine civil engineer Dana Humphrey, who was investigating whether the unusual properties of shredded rubber could be put to work inside a road structure.The material was not being used as a replacement for the road surface. Instead, it formed a layer beneath conventional gravel. The chips were intended to change what happened below the surface, rather than provide the wearing surface on which vehicles travelled.As reported by Los Angeles Times, a section of Dingley Road in Richmond became the site of a winter-long experiment. About 20,000 discarded tyres were cut into pieces roughly 2 to 3 inches across. The pieces still contained their steel belts.They were spread across a 600-foot section of the road, forming a layer between about 6 and 12 inches thick. Gravel was then placed above them in successive layers, eventually creating a conventional-looking road surface.Reportedly, the experiment was closely monitored. More than 100 temperature sensors were installed at different depths within the roadbed by Robert A. Eaton of the US Army Corps of Engineers Cold Regions Research & Engineering Laboratory. The sensors were connected to computers in Hanover, New Hampshire, allowing temperatures inside the road structure to be recorded throughout the winter.By spring, the tyre-chip section was behaving differently from nearby portions made entirely with gravel. Frost had penetrated to roughly half the depth observed in the comparison sections, while the gravel-only portions deteriorated badly during the thaw.Tyre chips have a physical advantage over ordinary road aggregate: they are much lighter. Gravel weighs about 125 pounds per cubic foot, whereas the tyre material used in the experiments weighed around 40 pounds.That difference can become important when large quantities of fill are needed. A lighter material places less weight on the soil below it, which makes the approach particularly interesting for construction on weak ground.Rubber also behaves differently from mineral soil when temperatures change. It does not transfer heat as readily, giving the chips an insulating quality. At the same time, the irregular pieces leave spaces through which water can move.The three characteristics: low weight, insulation and drainage made the material useful for more than just keeping frost out of a road.Humphrey and two graduate students also began constructing a retaining wall on the University of Maine campus. The planned structure was about 15 feet high and was intended to explore whether tyre chips could serve as lightweight fill behind a wall.That application had implications for places where conventional earth fill puts substantial pressure on slopes or retaining structures. Humphrey suggested that the method could have uses on steep roads in Southern California, where reducing the weight of material placed against a hillside could be useful in managing problems associated with unstable slopes.The concept was different from using finely ground rubber in asphalt. Crumb rubber had already been incorporated into some highway paving, but it required a much more processed product and was considerably more expensive.For one mile of interstate resurfacing in Maine, the material reportedly accounted for about 6,000 tyres, at a cost exceeding $20 per tyre. Using larger tyre pieces as fill could consume far greater quantities without requiring the same degree of grinding.The engineering experiment was taking place against a substantial waste problem. Maine residents were estimated to discard about 1.2 million tyres each year. Some ended up stored in large piles, including abandoned stockpiles that created environmental and fire concerns. Tyres can hold rainwater, providing places for mosquitoes to breed, while large tyre fires can burn for long periods and produce difficult-to-manage smoke.The state's recycling policy had also been shaped by legal and environmental problems surrounding two enormous tyre stockpiles. Government authorities were eventually placed in the position of dealing with the sites, adding pressure to find uses for tyres after disposal.For recyclers, however, finding an outlet was not necessarily the difficult part of collecting them. The market for products made from old tyres was still relatively small. In many cases, the disposal service itself generated more revenue than the sale of recycled material.Some tyres were already being burned for energy. Maine had waste-to-energy facilities that could use tyre chips, while a paper mill also used them as fuel. But preparing the material for combustion brought its own costs, particularly because the steel had to be removed as far as possible and the rubber needed to be cut into smaller pieces.The Richmond experiment used a gravel surface, so it did not answer every question about how tyre chips would perform beneath an ordinary paved road.That was the purpose of a planned test in North Yarmouth. An asphalt-topped section of highway was due to be constructed later that summer, providing an opportunity to see whether the material could perform beneath a conventional pavement under traffic.Earlier tests had indicated that once the chips were compacted using ordinary road-building equipment, they could support the loads imposed by heavy lorries.
Article Summary: 20,000 discarded tyres were cut into large chips and placed beneath a conventional gravel surface. When spring arrived, the experimental section showed noticeably less frost penetration and deterioration than nearby parts of the road. Maine's roads face a difficult seasonal cycle, with winter freezing the ground and spring thaw turning it soft and unstable.

Article Title: Watch: Zohran Mamdani look-alike contest draws hundreds in New York
Article Text:
Hundreds gathered near Washington Square Park on Sunday for a Zohran Mamdani look-alike contest. (Photo: @Complex_)

Contestants recreate Mamdani's campaign and cycling looks

Permit issue moves contest outside park

Mamdani impersonation becomes paying work

Amadeo Fusca, winner of the Zohran Mamdani look-alike contest, reacts with the crowd. (Photo: AP)

Hundreds gathered near Washington Square Park on Sunday for a Zohran Mamdani look-alike contest that drew on different phases of the New York mayor's public life, from politics and basketball to cycling and his earlier rap career.Actor and comedian Amadeo Fusca, 40, won the $100 prize in a New York Knicks jersey paired with formalwear, a Mamdani-style haircut and similar facial hair. His outfit echoed one worn by the mayor after the Knicks' NBA Finals victory.There was no judging panel. Each contestant named his favourite pizza before the crowd settled the result by applause.Silver rings, red-and-black ties and variations on dark formalwear appeared across the field, while some entrants drew on the brown suit Mamdani wore during his 2025 mayoral campaign.Others added bicycle helmets, referencing a more recent episode involving the mayor. Mamdani began wearing one earlier in August after facing criticism for cycling without a helmet.One entrant wore an apron with no shirt, drawing on imagery from Mamdani's 2019 Mr. Cardamom era.A permit issue forced a change of venue. The gathering began inside Washington Square Park, but police moved it beyond the park boundary because no permit had been obtained.Sonder, a social platform for meeting new people, sponsored the event.Mamdani, a democratic socialist whose political agenda has focused on New York's working class, took office in January and has built a substantial following among younger residents and on social media.Sunday's contest was not the first devoted to him. A similar event was held in Brooklyn during his 2025 run for City Hall.Washington Square Park has also hosted other look-alike competitions. In June, five-year-old Knicks fan Francisco won $5,000 at a Jalen Brunson look-alike contest there and received a surprise FaceTime call from Brunson, the NBA Finals MVP.Fusca had already turned his resemblance to Mamdani into a recurring act before entering Sunday's contest. The actor, who has appeared in episodes of “NCIS” and the film “The Alto Knights,” has drawn millions of views with social-media sketches impersonating the mayor.He said the act began during Mamdani's mayoral campaign, when friends repeatedly sent him photographs pointing out their resemblance. “It was kind of the perfect storm of people constantly hitting me up,” Fusca told the New York Post after his win.At first, he was reluctant to alter his appearance, particularly because he had been growing his hair.“The funny thing is, I was growing my hair, and I was like, ‘No, I’m growing my hair, I don’t really want to do that.’ And then when [Mamdani] won [the mayor’s race], it was just insane, the messages I was getting,” he said. “I went to the barber that morning and said, ‘Here, cut my hair, and make me look like this now.’ And like, I have to look like this all the time now!”The impersonation later began drawing attention at Knicks watch parties. Fusca, who lives only a few blocks from Gracie Mansion on Manhattan's Upper East Side, said the reactions exceeded what he had expected. “People were reacting like crazy, beyond what I even thought,” he said. “We just kept going to watch parties, and I kept inhabiting this field of people. It’s crazy how happy people get.”The attention has also begun translating into professional work. “I started doing Instagram videos to parody him and take on his shape,” Fusca said. “It started to get more love, and I sort of realized recently that people are hiring me to do their variety shows.”
Article Summary: Hundreds gathered near Washington Square Park on Sunday for a Zohran Mamdani look-alike contest. Actor and comedian Amadeo Fusca, 40, won the $100 prize in a New York Knicks jersey paired with formalwear. The contest drew on different phases of the New York mayor's public life, from politics and basketball to cycling.

Article Title: Melinda French Gates donated $10M to Olivia Rodrigo's Daisy Chain Fields Festival, bringing the total to $20M, here's where the money will be going
Article Text:
Baby2Baby provides children in need with diapers, clothing and basic necessities.

Black Mamas Matter Alliance aims to address maternal health inequities among Black women and improve their maternal health

Centre for Reproductive Rights is a legal organisation protecting reproductive rights and reproductive health globally

FreeFrom works to end gender-based violence and offers programs centred around finances and cash assistance

Jhpeigo aims to improve access to critical health care globally

Johns Hopkins Centre for Indigenous Health promotes health equity for Indigenous people

National Domestic Workers Alliance works to win labour rights and protections for domestic workers

National Institute for Reproductive Health partners with state and local advocates to provide strategic guidance, support and funding for access to reproductive health care

National Women's Law Centre advocates for 'gender justice' through courts and in public policy

Planned Parenthood provides sexual and reproductive health care for people nationwide

Trust the women in the world to make change and they will. Singer, songwriter Olivia Rodrigo successfully concluded her inaugural Daisy Chain Fields Festival on Saturday, August 29, in Irvine, California. The star-studded event included performances from artists such as Stevie Nicks , Karen O, Chappell Roan, Doechii, Bikini Kill, Rachel Chinouriri, Garbage, The Breeders and Mitski.The festival was inspired by Lilith Fair, which was co-founded by Sarah McLachlan in 1997 in response to the misogyny she and her peers were facing in the music industry. At the event, Rodrigo announced that they had raised $20M for women-focused organisations, aided by a donation from Melinda French Gates.Before she began her performance, Rodrigo thanked all of the musicians who took part in the festival: “The fact that they took the time out of their insanely busy schedules to come and do this festival for free is something I’m so grateful for,” she said. “Because of that, and because of all of you who came to hang out today, I can stand on the stage and say we are donating $10m to 10 incredible charities. I really believe that giving women the tools to decide their own futures and live healthy lives free of violence and discrimination is the most effective tool we have at changing the world for the better. ”Rodrigo then introduced Melinda French Gates, praising her as “one of the most inspiring women I’ve ever met”.“She’s devoted her life to empowering women and girls that might have otherwise been forgotten,” Rodrigo said. “She’s generous and brave and has done so much good in this world, and I’m totally floored because as well as being in attendance here tonight, she’s pledged to double every dollar that we made here today to a grand total of funds being donated to $20m. I’m so grateful!”Funds raised through the festival will be split equally among 10 beneficiary organisations: Baby2Baby, Black Mamas Matter Alliance, Centre for Reproductive Rights, FreeFrom, Jhpiego, John Hopkins Centre for Indigenous Health, National Domestic Workers Alliance, National Institute for Reproductive Health, National Women’s Law Centre, and Planned Parenthood.Here's what the organisations do:Rodrigo said the organisations are doing "incredibly important work every single day in the U.S. and globally." "I'm so grateful to every person who bought a ticket, every artist who waived their fee, every sponsor for signing onto a brand new festival and every donation that helped get to $10 million to support women and girls," she said.The event came as US President Donald Trump attempted to overhaul family planning grants that reproductive health clinics used to provide birth control and treat sexually transmitted infections. His administration paused $27.5 million last year for such organisations, including some Planned Parenthood affiliates, before officials agreed to restore the money.Rodrigo and her festival co-organisers have hinted that the event will return, as a post to its Instagram page showed the huge crowds in attendance with the caption: “One year down, and we’ll just keep growing.”
Article Summary: Singer, songwriter Olivia Rodrigo successfully concluded her inaugural Daisy Chain Fields Festival on Saturday, August 29, in Irvine, California. The star- studded event included performances from artists such as Stevie Nicks, Karen O, Chappell Roan, Doechii, Bikini Kill, Rachel Chinouriri, Garbage, The Breeders and Mitski. At the event, Rodrigo announced that they had raised $20M for women- focused organisations, aided by a donation from Melinda French Gates.

Article Title: A San Antonio storm knocked out power and damaged homes; one barber simply moved his chair outside and kept cutting customers’ hair
Article Text:
Martinez moved a barber’s chair outside the shop and continued cutting customers’ hair. (Photo: TPR)

No electricity stops this barber

Strong winds and heavy rain swept through the area Friday evening. (Photo: San Antonio Express News)

West Side residents help each other

A powerful storm knocked out power and damaged homes across San Antonio on Friday night, but a barber refused to close his shop. Texas Publilc Radio reported that with no electricity, he moved his barber chair outside and continued cutting customers’ hair as residents cleaned up fallen trees and dealt with the heat.Winds of 50 to 65 mph, heavy rain, lightning and flash flooding to parts of the city knocked down trees and power lines across the city, left homes damaged, trees and utility poles toppled and more than 112,000 CPS Energy customers without electricity at its peak.Tens of thousands of people were still without power on Saturday as residents began clearing debris and checking the damage. With temperatures rising towards 100 degrees, families without electricity also had to find ways to stay cool.On San Antonio’s West Side, the morning after the storm was filled with the sounds of chainsaws, generators and people working together. Streets near Zarzamora Street were covered with fallen branches and trees. Some trees had landed on homes and vehicles, while others brought down power lines.The power cuts also affected businesses across the West Side. Some businesses closed on Saturday, while others looked for ways to continue operating despite the outage.At the Misfit barbershop on Martin Street, owner and barber Juan Martinez decided not to close. Instead, he moved a barber’s chair outside the shop and continued cutting customers’ hair.The chair was placed beneath an awning, where it had some shade. The shop itself had no electricity, but Martinez was determined to keep working. “It’s a hard time, but you want to look good,” Martinez said.For Martinez, closing was not really an option. “I’m a business owner and as long as I’m out here showing my guys, power, no power, we can still do it,” he said.A little wind outside was enough to make the arrangement possible, Martinez said. His customers were also trying to deal with the situation in the same way.“It’s hard, it’s crazy, it’s difficult, but at the end of the day all they say is we gotta roll with the punches. We gotta keep positive.”The damage around the neighbourhood was still clearly visible. Fallen trees had hit vehicles and power lines, while some homes had roofs badly damaged or completely removed.“These trees are old and you see them and the trees are knocked over the vehicles, knocked out powerlines, there’s a couple of houses where the roofs are caved in, roofs are taken off, it’s just madness right now,” Martinez said.Despite the damage and power outages, Martinez said the neighbourhood had an important strength- its community. “I feel like as a community we can pull together,” he said.Martinez was born and raised on the West Side and said the area’s history and roots were an important part of its identity.“That’s what I love about the West Side,” he said. “I’m born and raised over here. The West Side has history. You have roots down here. You have a foundation of who you are.”Residents spent Saturday dealing with the immediate effects of the storm. Some cut up fallen trees, others cleared damaged homes, while families without electricity tried to stay cool.
Article Summary: Winds of 50 to 65 mph, heavy rain, lightning and flash flooding to parts of the city knocked down trees and power lines across the city. More than 112,000 CPS Energy customers without electricity at its peak. Businesses closed on Saturday, while others looked for ways to continue operating despite the outage.

Article Title: 'Venezuela will be reborn': Maduro shares first photos from US prison since capture
Article Text:
Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro smiles and flashes a peace sign in a photograph. (Photo: @NicolasMaduro)

Oil deal widens US role in Venezuela

Defence prepares immunity challenge

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe Maduro can receive a fair trial in the US? Definitely, the legal system works. No, there's too much bias. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Two photographs posted to Nicolás Maduro's official social-media accounts on Sunday appear to show the former Venezuelan president smiling and making peace signs at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, nearly eight months after US forces captured him in Caracas.The pictures show the 63-year-old dressed in a grey sweatshirt and trousers with white shoes. Although released on August 30, timestamps on the photographs indicate they were taken on June 25.“I send these photos as a small gift to all my grandsons and granddaughters, to the boys and girls, and to all the noble people who love us,” Maduro said in an English rendering of his Spanish-language message. He said he and his wife, Cilia Flores, would “remain strong, serene, and confident” and added: “Venezuela will be reborn.” Maduro also described the support reaching the couple as “that love that reaches us transformed into prayer, into constant action, into solidarity and true support. ”The June 25 date places the photographs a day after two earthquakes measuring magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 struck Venezuela. The death toll from the quakes had risen to 6,509 by August 25.Maduro's message emerged as the government led by acting President Delcy Rodríguez moves into a new phase of relations with Washington, particularly over Venezuela's vast oil reserves.President Donald Trump said on Friday that the United States had secured majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela's proven oil reserves through a partnership with private business.Rodríguez subsequently said the bilateral energy project would run for 25 years and involve 17 strategic oilfields, with an initial production target of more than 1.5 million barrels a day, news agency Reuters reported.News agency Associated Press separately reported, citing a US official familiar with the agreement, that the new private company had been granted 100-year rights to develop the oilfields.Several important terms have yet to be made public. The US official told AP that the United States would receive 55% of the effective output of the new company through a combination of an ownership stake and rights to buy oil at cost. It remains unclear how much of that share would come from equity ownership and how much from the oil-purchase arrangement.Questions also remain over how the agreement will be financed and implemented, while the identity of the private operator has not been disclosed.Trump said on Sunday that Venezuelan crude obtained through the arrangement would also be used to replenish the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The stockpile held about 290 million barrels on August 21, near its lowest level in 44 years.A substantial increase in Venezuelan production is unlikely to come quickly. The country's oil infrastructure requires major investment, while unresolved financing and legal questions could affect how rapidly companies commit capital.While relations between Caracas and Washington have shifted since Maduro's removal, he and Flores remain in US custody awaiting a trial scheduled for June 1, 2027.US forces seized the couple from their Caracas residence during an overnight operation authorised by Trump on January 3 and transferred them to New York. They appeared in federal court two days later and pleaded not guilty.Maduro faces four felony counts, including narcoterrorism conspiracy and conspiracy to import cocaine. Federal prosecutors accuse him of involvement in a scheme to facilitate cocaine shipments to the United States. He could face life in prison if convicted.His lawyer, Barry Pollack, has said he will seek dismissal on the ground that Maduro is immune from prosecution as the head of a sovereign state. Pollack has also previously indicated that the defence may challenge the legality of Maduro's capture.US District Judge Alvin Hellerstein has given the defence until September 2 to file its first round of motions seeking dismissal. Arguments on those motions are scheduled for November 17, while a second round of motions is due by January 11, 2027, after prosecutors turn over additional evidence, some of which is expected to be classified.
Article Summary: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro appears to make peace signs in photos posted to his official social-media accounts on Sunday. The pictures show the 63-year-old dressed in a grey sweatshirt and trousers with white shoes. He and his wife, Cilia Flores, remain in US custody awaiting a trial scheduled for June 1, 2027.

Article Title: ‘Blown to smithereens’: Trump shares AI-generated video of Iran’s Kharg Island
Article Text:
Image credit: Donald Trump's Truth social

Strait of Hormuz faces renewed disruption

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe the U.S. military action in Iran is justified? Yes No 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that Iran's Kharg Island was being “blown to smithereens”, without providing details, as tensions between Washington and Tehran escalated after the first known US strikes on Iran in weeks.Kharg Island is a major Iranian energy hub that handled about 90% of the country's oil exports before the war began with US and Israeli attacks on February 28. Any significant damage to the island could disrupt Iran's oil trade and place further pressure on its economy."Kharg Island being blown to smithereens!!! President DJT," Trump said on social media.The White House and US Defense Department did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. Reuters also verified that an accompanying video showing dramatic explosions had been artificially generated.The U.S. strikes earlier hit two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. Central Command said it had taken "limited, precise" action against Iranian Revolutionary Guard minelaying forces that posed an "imminent threat" in the strategic waterway.The command did not provide further details.Iran subsequently launched ballistic missiles towards two U.S. bases in Jordan, Iranian media reported. Jordan's armed forces said they had intercepted eight missiles that entered its airspace.A Fox News reporter, citing a U.S. source, said nearly all incoming missiles "have been intercepted at this point", indicating limited immediate impact.Iran's Revolutionary Guards said the attack killed and wounded several soldiers and civilians and vowed a "response and punishment" from Tehran, according to Iranian state media.The escalation has also raised fresh concerns over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global energy supplies.The number of visible commodity vessels crossing the waterway fell to about five a day over the weekend, according to shipping data. The actual number could be higher because some vessels have switched off their automatic identification systems to avoid potential attacks.Trump said last week that all mines in the international waters of the strait had either been detonated or removed, and warned Iran that any vessel laying new mines would be destroyed.While Trump has repeatedly said the waterway remains open, Iran's Revolutionary Guards' navy has rejected that claim as "an obvious lie", saying the strait remains closed to ships without Iranian permission.The Strait of Hormuz carried nearly one-fifth of global crude oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before it was blockaded during the six-month-old Iran war.Iran is the third-largest producer in the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries.
Article Summary: U.S. Central Command said it had taken "limited, precise" action against Iranian Revolutionary Guard minelaying forces. Kharg Island is a major Iranian energy hub that handled about 90% of the country's oil exports before the war began with US and Israeli attacks on February 28.

Article Title: A New Orleans couple found a 1,900-year-old Roman sailor’s gravestone buried in their backyard; it had vanished from an Italian museum during WWII and has now returned home
Article Text:
1,900-year-old Roman gravestone discovered in a New Orleans backyard in 2025 has returned to the Italian city of Civitavecchia where it soon be put on public display.

A Roman tombstone, lurking in New Orleans

The archeological mystery unveiled

Taking it home through international collaboration

An old story, a new chapter

Sometimes, a normal backyard hides a piece of history that has traveled further than anyone could ever imagine. A report published by Tulane University state that a couple in New Orleans recently unearthed a marble gravestone beneath their property that was almost 2,000 years old and absent from an Italian museum since the chaos of World War II. Now, the incredible find has come full circle, with the ancient Roman artifact being returned to the Italian city where it was first discovered. Scroll down to read the details.According to the University website, the marble tablet, dating from the second century A.D., commemorates Sextus Congenius Verus, a sailor who served in the Praetorian fleet based at Misenum near Naples. It was first discovered in 1866 near the old Roman port city of Centumcellae, today called Civitavecchia. It then passed into the collection of the city’s civic museum. But the story took a turn during the Second World War. The gravestone was lost from the collection and the museum was destroyed. For decades scholars had thought the ancient monument was lost forever until March 2025 and was then found in the backyard. The stone was found by anthropologist Daniella Santoro, of Tulane University, and her husband, Aaron Lorenz, as they worked in the backyard of their home in New Orleans.They took note of the odd slab because it had Latin inscriptions. Santoro contacted Susann S. Lusnia, a professor of classical studies at Tulane University, to see if she could help identify it.Lusnia immediately recognized the lettering and language to be consistent with an authentic Roman funerary inscription. She started searching scholarly databases with words from the inscription. The research soon produced a surprising result: the stone seemed to be the same monument that had been documented in Civitavecchia before vanishing in the Second World War.It was a remarkable moment of identification for Lusnia. The inscription was more than an ancient Roman object. It was a known object, with a known history, so it was possible to follow its path from Roman antiquity to an Italian museum and finally to an American backyard. Once the connection was established, Lusnia reached out to colleagues in Italy, and helped to set up communications with the National Archeological Museum of Civitavecchia. The find quickly grabbed international attention as historians, archeologists and the public became intrigued by the mystery of how a nearly 1,900-year-old Roman monument had come to New Orleans.The final return of the artifact involved a number of organizations on both sides of the Atlantic.
