The FBI Art Crime Team collaborated with the Consulate General of Italy in New York, the Italian Carabinieri Command for the Protection of Cultural Heritage, and Italian judicial authorities. The owners have agreed to return the tablet to Italy voluntarily. The ancient gravestone was returned in April 2026, according to the required procedures. The artifact has been cleaned and returned to the collection from which it was missing for more than 80 years.The gravestone is being prepared for public exhibition at the National Archeological Museum of Civitavecchia. It will be one of the featured artifacts when the museum reopens September 18 after a massive renovation. The new museum will display archeological artifacts, multimedia presentations and interactive exhibits that illustrate more than 3,000 years of Civitavecchia’s history. The importance of the return of the tablet is not only for its age, but for the return of a key element of the city’s archeological heritage. For Lusnia, the journey is a powerful reminder that history can emerge in the most unexpected of places. An artifact missing since 1943 survived generations intact before turning up thousands of miles away, waiting to be recognized. A Roman sailor’s gravestone has come home, as a reminder that even after almost 2,000 years and decades of being lost, the past can find its way back.
Article Summary: The marble tablet, dating from the second century A.D., commemorates Sextus Congenius Verus, a sailor who served in the Praetorian fleet based at Misenum near Naples. It was first discovered in 1866 near the old Roman port city of Centumcellae, today called Civitavecchia. It then passed into the collection of the city’s civic museum. But the story took a turn during the Second World War. The gravestone was lost from the collection and the museum was destroyed. For decades scholars had thought the ancient monument was lost forever

Article Title: After losing their Los Angeles home in the wildfire, a California family bought a $1 historic house and moved it onto their burned property
Article Text:
Lauren Martinez and Morgan Sykes Jaybush, creative director of the architectural firm Omgivning, at Martinez's relocated home. Image Credit: Gary Leonard/ Omgivning

How did a $1 house become new home for the California family

Martinez purchased this 100-year-old home in Hollywood for $1. Image Credit Omgivning

What happened to the Martinez family’s original home

Moving an entire house across Los Angeles

Relocation, instead of demolition of the historic houses

What happens to ‘Pinky’ next

A California family has found a unique way to rebuild after losing its Altadena home in the devastating Eaton fire. Instead of constructing a new house, it bought a nearly 100-years-old historic home for just $1 and moved it to the burned property. The house, nicknamed ‘Pinky,’ was facing demolition in Hollywood before the family stepped in to save it. The 2,500-square-foot Tudor Revival home was divided into two sections, transported 26 miles by truck and placed on the family’s empty lot. This remarkable move is part of the ‘Historic House Relocation Project,’ an initiative designed to preserve older Los Angeles homes while helping families displaced by wildfires. For the Martinez family, this solution offered a larger home filled with historic character, while giving an endangered house another chance to become part of a community again.Lauren Martinez and her husband learned about the Historic House Relocation Project, launched by Los Angeles architecture firm ‘Omgivning’ in 2025. The project finds older homes that are facing demolition and matches them with families rebuilding after the wildfires.The idea is relatively simple, even if the actual work is not. A house that might otherwise be demolished is purchased, carefully taken apart or divided into sections, transported to another property and then restored. For the Martinezes, the right house was a nearly 100-years-old Tudor Revival property in Hollywood. It had been well maintained and still featured hardwood floors throughout. The one-storey house measured about 2,500 square feet and contained four bedrooms and three bathrooms. Most remarkably, the family bought it for only $1. They gave the house a nickname ‘Pinky’ that reflected how quickly it became part of the family and because it was pink inside and out. Martinez said that the house felt as though it carried years of love and character with it.The Martinez family had lived in their Altadena home for 8 years and were raising their children, when the Eaton fire destroyed it in January 2025. Lauren Martinez was eight months pregnant with her third child when she received messages warning her to stay away from the neighbourhood. The following day, her husband saw the smouldering rubble of their family home. The family later found themselves living in a rental while considering how to rebuild. But the financial reality made a traditional replacement difficult. According to Realtor, Martinez said insurance would not have provided enough money to recreate the home they had lost at the same size. Building again would have meant accepting a smaller, simpler house. That pushed the family to consider a very different option of moving an existing historic house onto their land.Moving a house is considerably more complicated than transporting ordinary furniture. The Martinez project required months of planning involving architects, contractors and specialist movers. The house had to be divided along what was considered its most suitable natural seam. Omgivning creative director ‘Morgan Sykes Jaybush’ compared the process to slicing a loaf of bread. Each half then had to be prepared for transport and moved separately. On 12 January 2026, the first half was secured with wood, mounted on steel beams and placed on a flatbed tractor-trailer. It travelled 26 miles from Hollywood to Altadena during the night. Four days later, the second half made the same journey. The Los Angeles Conservancy reports that the wider Historic House Relocation Project requires careful evaluation and documentation before a house is moved. Once relocated, each property needs a new foundation and must be rehabilitated to meet modern building codes while retaining its historic character.The project is tackling two problems at once. According to the Los Angeles Conservancy, many older homes in LA face demolition as neighbourhoods change and redevelopment takes place. At the same time, families affected by the Eaton and Palisades fires need ways to rebuild without losing the character of their communities. The relocation project connects those two needs. Rather than allowing an older house to disappear, it gives the building a new site and a new family. The Los Angeles Conservancy reports that three early relocations include the 1911 Chambers Residence, the 1910 Duntley-Blackburn Residence and the 1926 Martinez Residence. According to Realtor, Omgivning has helped three families relocate homes so far, while around 200 people are on its waiting list. The project’s organisers estimate that the approach can be about 20% cheaper than constructing a new home on average, while also saving older houses from demolition.Although the house has reached the Martinez family’s Altadena property, the work is far from finished. The building is currently resting on temporary supports while a new foundation is prepared. Plumbing and electrical systems must be installed, the two sections need to be joined, and the roof, which was removed before the move, must be rebuilt. The kitchen will also be renovated. Martinez expects the entire project to cost between $900,000-$950,000. Even so, she believes building a new house from scratch would have taken longer and potentially cost considerably more. Most importantly, the relocated home gives the family the character of an older house. After watching their old home disappear in the fire, they are now waiting for a house with its own history to become their new beginning.
Article Summary: The Martinez family lost their Altadena home in the Eaton fire in January 2025. Lauren Martinez and her husband learned about the Historic House Relocation Project, launched by Los Angeles architecture firm ‘Omgivning’ The project finds older homes that are facing demolition and matches them with families rebuilding after the wildfires. A house that might otherwise be demolished is purchased, carefully taken apart or divided into sections, transported to another property and then restored. For the Martinez family, this solution offered a larger home filled with historic character, while giving an endangered house another chance to become part of a community again.

Article Title: Alaska used rotenone to eliminate invasive pike from an entire lake; the pike vanished, and 6,836 Arctic char were later stocked to rebuild the native fishery
Article Text:
Representative image

Why northern pike are a problem in Alaska

Rotenone: a targeted, temporary reset

Alaska eliminates invasive pike and restocks lake with 6,836 Arctic char

Stormy Lake: a case study in eradication and recovery

Other lakes, similar stories

Why Arctic char matter

Balancing restoration with public concern

A tool, not a silver bullet

In a remote corner of Southcentral Alaska, state biologists carried out a dramatic restoration: they treated an entire lake with rotenone, a plant-derived piscicide, to wipe out an invasive population of northern pike. After the treatment, post-surveys confirmed the pike were gone. The next step was rebuilding what had been lost. In June 2013, the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) stocked 6,836 hatchery-reared Arctic char fingerlings into the now pike-free lake, jump-starting the recovery of a native fishery that had been pushed out by the predator. This account draws on ADF&G’s technical reports and project summaries documenting the rotenone treatment and restocking. Read on to know more:Northern pike are not native to most of Southcentral Alaska. They were illegally introduced into several lakes in the mid-20th century and have since spread through connected waterways, especially as warming temperatures and changing hydrology make it easier for them to move and survive. As apex predators, pike eat large quantities of native fish, including salmon, trout, grayling and char. In some lakes, they have all but replaced native sport fish, collapsing local angling opportunities and altering food webs.ADF&G describes pike as a major threat to endemic fish populations and has pursued a mix of suppression and eradication strategies depending on the waterbody. In isolated lakes where pike can be completely removed, the agency has turned to rotenone as the most practical and efficient tool.Rotenone is a naturally occurring compound derived from certain tropical plants. It has been used for decades in fisheries management to remove unwanted fish from lakes and streams. When applied at carefully calculated concentrations, it blocks oxygen uptake in fish gills, killing fish while leaving most other aquatic organisms unaffected. The chemical breaks down relatively quickly in sunlight and warm water; in many Alaskan projects, detectable levels drop to near zero within weeks to months.There are only two proven methods to eradicate invasive fish from lakes: completely draining the waterbody or using a piscicide like rotenone. For most lakes, draining is not feasible, making rotenone the default option for full eradication. Before treatment, ADF&G typically relocates any desirable native fish, such as salmon or trout, to safe holding areas or other lakes, then treats the target lake and its outlet streams to ensure no pike survive.Stormy Lake, near Anchorage, is one of the clearest examples of this approach. In fall 2012, ADF&G treated Stormy Lake and its outlet creek with liquid rotenone to eradicate an established northern pike population. Post-treatment evaluations—including netting and electrofishing surveys, found no surviving pike, confirming the treatment’s success.Once the rotenone had fully degraded (by late January 2013, about four months after application), the agency began restocking. Native fish that had been held in offsite net pens were reintroduced in March 2013, and on June 17, 2013, ADF&G stocked 6,836 hatchery-reared Arctic char fingerlings into Stormy Lake. These char were of mixed Stormy Lake and Dolly Varden Lake parentage, helping to re-establish a robust, genetically diverse population.The project’s final report, published in ADF&G’s Sport Fish Research series, describes the effort as a successful model for eradicating invasive pike and restoring native fisheries.Stormy Lake is not unique. ADF&G has used rotenone to remove pike from multiple lakes in the Anchorage and Mat-Su areas, including Sand Lake, Anderson Lake and Kings Lake. In each case, the sequence is similar: treat the lake, confirm pike are gone, then restock with native species such as rainbow trout, Arctic char and grayling.For example, after rotenone treatments in 2020, Anderson and Kings lakes were declared pike-free and added to the Northern Cook Inlet stocking program in 2021. Both lakes were restocked with rainbow trout, restoring sport fisheries that had been lost to pike predation. In Anchorage, pike have been eradicated from all but one of five lakes where they were confirmed, with Lower Fire Lake remaining a management challenge.Arctic char are a prized native species in Alaska, valued both ecologically and by anglers. They thrive in cold, clear lakes and are an important part of the natural food web. In lakes where pike have been removed, char are often a key restocking target because they can grow to good size, support recreational fishing and help re-establish a more natural predator–prey balance.In Stormy Lake, the 6,836 char stocked in 2013 were intended to re-create a self-sustaining population that could eventually support a catch-and-release or limited-harvest fishery. Monitoring in subsequent years showed that char, along with other restocked natives, were surviving and growing, indicating the lake was returning to a healthier, pre-pike state.The use of rotenone is not without controversy. Killing all fish in a lake, even temporarily, can be unsettling for nearby residents and anglers. ADF&G addresses these concerns through public meetings, environmental assessments and detailed explanations of why the treatment is necessary and how risks are managed.Agency biologists emphasise that the alternative, allowing pike to remain, is often worse for native biodiversity and long-term fishing opportunities. In lakes where pike have taken hold, native species may never recover without a full reset. Rotenone, used correctly, offers a way to hit that reset button and then rebuild the fishery with native species.While rotenone has proven effective in isolated lakes, it is not a solution for every pike-infested waterbody. In large, connected systems like much of the Mat-Su Valley, complete eradication is currently impossible because pike can simply move back in from untreated areas. There, ADF&G focuses on suppression, using gillnets, targeted rotenone applications in key tributaries, and liberal harvest rules to keep pike numbers down in priority fisheries.Projects like Stormy Lake show where eradication is still feasible: in relatively closed basins where pike can be fully removed and native fish reintroduced. For those lakes, the combination of rotenone treatment and strategic stocking—like the 6,836 Arctic char released in 2013, offers a path back to a more natural, resilient fishery. For Alaska’s fisheries managers, such projects demonstrate that invasive predators can sometimes be removed and native fish populations rebuilt when the conditions are right.
Article Summary: Northern pike are not native to most of Southcentral Alaska. They were illegally introduced into several lakes in the mid-20th century. Pike eat large quantities of native fish, including salmon, trout, grayling and char. They have all but replaced native sport fish, collapsing local angling opportunities.

Article Title: In 1940, actor James Cagney bought hundreds of acres of California grassland; decades later the remaining 417 acres became a protected wildlife corridor
Article Text:
How the Cagney brothers acquired the Ramona grasslands in the 1940s

AI Generated

How the Ramona grasslands kept habitats connected

Rare wildlife found across the Ramona grasslands

How the Ramona grasslands deal took six years to complete

How one purchase could protect more Ramona grasslands

What remained from the old ranch

For decades, the grasslands outside Ramona, California, looked much as they had for generations: open country, seasonal pools and wide stretches of native vegetation broken by grazing land. As reported by the local news report, The San Diego Union-Tribune, among the people who once owned part of this landscape was Hollywood actor James Cagney , who acquired hundreds of acres in the area with his brother William during the 1940s. The property did not remain intact forever. Portions were sold over the years, leaving 417 acres under the William J. Cagney Trust.By the early 2000s, however, the remaining tract had caught the attention of conservationists for a very different reason. It was part of one of the last sizable grassland habitats in coastal Southern California, supporting rare plants and threatened wildlife. In 2003, after years of negotiations, the Nature Conservancy purchased the former Cagney property for $2.7 million, placing the remaining land on a path toward long-term protection.Ramona was a very different place when the Cagney brothers acquired their land. The community was still relatively rural, and the grasslands stretched across a wide valley floor.The property was used as open country, with livestock grazing among native grasses and seasonal wetlands.Reportedly, James Cagney was already a major film star by this period, known for films such as The Public Enemy and Yankee Doodle Dandy. His brother William, however, had a separate connection to the property and remained associated with the Ramona holding.Accounts of the land differ slightly on the exact size of the original purchase, but later reporting put it at more than 500 acres. Over the following decades, portions were sold. What remained became the Cagney Ranch, held through the family trust.As reported, by the time conservation groups began seriously pursuing the property, the 417-acre remnant had become more significant than its size alone suggested.Large grassland valleys are not easy to preserve in coastal Southern California. Their flat terrain makes them attractive for roads, houses and other development, leaving relatively few expansive areas intact.The Ramona grasslands were one of those exceptions. The wider area covered thousands of acres and contained a mixture of grassland, vernal pools and other habitats. It also formed part of a larger network of open land extending through San Diego County. Conservation groups saw the remaining large parcels as opportunities to keep those connections intact rather than allowing the landscape to become increasingly fragmented.The Cagney property sat close to the centre of that effort. It was not an isolated patch of vegetation surrounded by development. Its position meant that protecting it could help connect other conservation areas and leave room for further acquisitions.The land also supported species that had become increasingly difficult to find elsewhere.The Nature Conservancy identified the Stephens' kangaroo rat, San Diego fairy shrimp and arroyo southwestern toad among the threatened or endangered species associated with the Ramona grasslands. Seasonal vernal pools on the Cagney property had also produced records of three rare plant species.Vernal pools are particularly distinctive features of the landscape. They fill during the wet season and then dry out, creating temporary aquatic habitats that can support species adapted to conditions found in few other places.For conservationists, preserving the surrounding grassland mattered as well. Wildlife does not necessarily remain inside the boundaries of a single protected parcel. Maintaining open ground between habitats can allow animals and plants to persist across a wider landscape.The Nature Conservancy did not simply arrive one day and purchase the ranch. The idea had been developing for years.Dave Bittner, executive director of the Wildlife Research Institute in Ramona, had first contacted the conservancy about the property in 1997. Discussions continued, and the acquisition began taking clearer shape around 2000.That long timeline was typical of large conservation purchases. Finding a willing seller was only one part of the process. Millions of dollars had to be assembled, different organisations had to coordinate their contributions, and the ecological value of the land had to be weighed against competing possibilities for its future.Reportedly, a federal grant helped move the proposal forward. The US Fish and Wildlife Service provided $660,000, while the state contributed another $165,000. The largest contribution, $1.236 million, came through California's Wildlife Conservation Board using funds from a statewide bond approved by voters in 2002.The Nature Conservancy put $639,000 of its own funds into the purchase. Escrow finally closed on June 30, 2003.The $2.7 million transaction protected 417 acres, but conservation groups were thinking beyond that single purchase.At the time, the Ramona grasslands covered roughly 8,000 acres and contained several large privately held parcels. The Cagney property helped connect existing conservation plans and offered a possible route towards a larger protected landscape.The Wildlife Research Institute, which owned 10 acres beside the southwest corner of the new preserve, intended to continue working towards protecting more of the grasslands. Its researchers had been documenting the area's wildlife and habitat for years.For them, the acquisition was a beginning rather than an endpoint.The broader conservation ambition was to keep substantial parts of the grassland intact while finding ways for development and habitat protection to coexist elsewhere. That was important in a county where coastal, mountain and desert environments meet, producing an unusually varied collection of habitats.The 417 acres carried a family name linked to one of Hollywood's most recognisable actors, but the property's significance eventually came from something far removed from the film industry.Pieces of the original Cagney holding had disappeared over the decades as land changed hands. The remaining parcel was the part that could still make a difference to the surrounding ecosystem.In 2003, the Nature Conservancy described it as one of the last remnants of grassland habitat in coastal Southern California. The purchase kept that section from following the same path as many other flat, developable pieces of the region.The landscape itself had not changed overnight. There was no new monument or dramatic transformation when the sale closed. Instead, ownership changed hands, and with it came a commitment to manage the property as part of a wider conservation effort.For a piece of land first acquired by the Cagney family decades earlier, that was a quiet but significant change in direction.
Article Summary: Hollywood actor James Cagney acquired hundreds of acres in the area with his brother William during the 1940s. The property did not remain intact forever. Portions were sold over the years, leaving 417 acres. Conservation groups saw the remaining large parcels as opportunities to keep those connections intact rather than allowing the landscape to become increasingly fragmented.

Article Title: Lahore inflation squeezes household budgets as food, rent and utility costs rise
Article Text:
People walk through a market to shop for grocery and other items

Vegetable, LPG prices add to public anger

Rising inflation in Pakistan's Lahore has intensified financial pressures on ordinary citizens, with soaring prices of food, rent, utilities and other essentials making it increasingly difficult for low-income families to make ends meet, new agency ANI reported.Residents said the rising cost of basic commodities has made it difficult for some households to afford even two meals a day. Prices of flour, cooking oil, pulses, vegetables and other necessities have continued to rise, while daily-wage workers and low-income earners said their incomes have failed to keep pace with inflation.Citizens also raised concerns over sharply higher vegetable prices, saying commonly consumed items such as potatoes and tomatoes have become increasingly unaffordable. Residents said vegetables were being sold for around Rs 150 to Rs 300 per kilogram, depending on the item and market.One resident appealed to the government to address the difficulties faced by poor families, saying rising food prices, rent and utility bills had made household management extremely challenging. Families on limited incomes, he said, were increasingly being forced to choose between food, rent, medicines and other essential expenses.ANI reports that people living on modest pensions were struggling to manage household expenses, particularly when they also had children, medical costs and other financial responsibilities.Residents also criticised the government over LPG prices, alleging that the fuel was being sold above official rates in some markets. They questioned who would regulate traders and ensure enforcement of government price controls.Rickshaw driver Usman Ali said rising fuel and essential commodity prices had severely affected his livelihood, leaving little or nothing to save after meeting basic household expenses.Citizens further questioned why lower petrol prices had not resulted in cheaper food and other essential commodities, asking why reductions in fuel costs were not being reflected in market prices.
Article Summary: Rising prices of food, rent, utilities and other essentials making it increasingly difficult for low-income families to make ends meet. Prices of flour, cooking oil, pulses, vegetables and other necessities have continued to rise. Citizens also raised concerns over sharply higher vegetable prices. Residents also criticised the government over LPG prices.

Article Title: Kabul, Kashmir, Mumbai, Pahalgam: Hafiz Saeed’s deadly four-decade terror trail
Article Text:
Four decades of Lashkar: How Hafiz Saeed’s network moved from Afghanistan to Kashmir (Associated press image)

LeT's major attacks

The Afghan war that created LeT's foundations

Deadly Embrace: Pakistan, America, and the Future of the Global Jihad

Why Lashkar-e-Taiba was established

From Kunar to Kashmir

Lashkar-e-Taiba: From 9/11 to Mumbai

Who is Hafiz Saeed

Hafiz Saeed - From cleric to terrorist

LeT survives Pakistani ban after 9/11

Four decades of evolution

From Kashmir insurgency to Mumbai

Why Afghanistan remained part of the network

Saeed's legal history and the Pahalgam case

From Afghan jihad to Kashmir

From Afghan jihad to Pahalgam

The legal case against Lashkar-e-Taiba founder Hafiz Muhammad Saeed has acquired a fresh dimension in India. In July 2026, the National Investigation Agency named Saeed in a supplementary chargesheet in the Pahalgam terror attack case, charging him in his individual capacity and as the founder and chief of Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) and its active proxy, The Resistance Front (TRF). The NIA mentioned a cross-border conspiracy behind the April 22, 2025 attack, which killed 26 civilians. A special NIA court subsequently issued a non-bailable warrant against Saeed.The development came as Mumbai Police separately began proceedings for a trial in absentia against Saeed and five other Pakistan-based accused in the 2008 Mumbai terror attacks. The proclamation covers Saeed, LeT operations chief Zaki-ur-Rehman Lakhvi, Sajid Mir, Abu Alqama, Asim alias Abu Qahafa and Major Abdur Rehman Pasha. The police have also approached the Union home ministry to facilitate service of the proclamation orders through Interpol.The two cases, separated by 17 years, bring together different phases of LeT's history. One concerns an attack in Kashmir, the region that became the organisation's principal battlefield in the 1990s. The other concerns the Mumbai attacks, which demonstrated how far LeT's operational reach had expanded beyond the Kashmir insurgency.But LeT did not begin in Kashmir, nor did Hafiz Saeed first emerge as a militant leader there. The organisation's institutional roots can be traced to the Afghan jihad of the 1980s, when Pakistan became a major centre for the mobilisation, training and movement of Islamist fighters.The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 created an environment in which Islamist networks from Pakistan and other parts of the Muslim world expanded rapidly. Among the prominent figures associated with this mobilisation was Palestinian scholar Abdullah Azzam, who helped organise foreign volunteers for the Afghan jihad and promoted the idea of jihad as a broader obligation extending beyond a single battlefield.It was in this environment that Azzam worked with Hafiz Saeed, a Pakistani Sunni scholar who had studied in Saudi Arabia. According to Bruce Riedel's, the two were involved in establishing Markaz-ud-Dawa-wal-Irshad (MDI), a religious organisation that combined missionary activity with support for jihad. MDI developed training infrastructure in Afghanistan, including in Kunar province, where recruits could gain battlefield experience. Riedel also records links between the organisation and Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI).Lashkar-e-Taiba subsequently emerged as the military wing associated with this network. The US state department describes LeT as having formed in the late 1980s as the militant wing of MDI, an organisation originally established in opposition to the Soviet presence in Afghanistan. The Australian government dates LeT's formation as a military organisation to 1989.The exact formation date therefore varies depending on whether the establishment of MDI, the creation of its military wing or the later formalisation of LeT is being referred to. What is clearer is the sequence: the Afghan jihad provided the organisation's early ideological, human and training infrastructure, while the end of the Soviet war opened the way for that infrastructure to be redirected towards other conflicts.LeT's early purpose was shaped by two connected objectives: participation in the Afghan jihad and preparation for jihad in Kashmir and India. Riedel describes MDI's objective as applying the experience of the Afghan war to Kashmir and India, including training Kashmiris alongside Afghan mujahideen so they could gain combat experience.The changing situation in Afghanistan accelerated that transition. The Soviet withdrawal meant that the battlefield that had brought together thousands of militants was no longer the same. At the same time, violence in Jammu and Kashmir was rising sharply.The Australian government's account of LeT's history says the organisation was originally formed to wage militant jihad against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan and shifted its focus to the insurgency in Indian-administered Kashmir during the 1990s after Soviet troops withdrew. It identifies the organisation's stated objective as uniting Kashmir with Pakistan, while noting that its broader ideological objectives extended beyond Kashmir.Kashmir thus became the next major theatre in which the organisation could deploy the personnel, training and networks developed during the Afghan war.The shift towards Kashmir coincided with the rapid growth of the insurgency there. Riedel records that incidents of violence in Kashmir rose from 390 in 1988 to 2,100 in 1989 and nearly 4,000 in 1990. Against this backdrop, Saeed's organisation began establishing infrastructure in and around Kashmir while maintaining training facilities in Pakistan and Afghanistan.LeT's emergence also coincided with changes among the various groups fighting in Kashmir. The Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front advocated an independent Kashmir, while Pakistan's security establishment increasingly favoured groups committed to the territory's integration with Pakistan. Riedel describes efforts to strengthen pro-Pakistan organisations and isolate the JKLF, which was regarded as too independent. Hizbul Mujahideen became a major pro-Pakistan militant force, while LeT developed its own network and capabilities.By the 1990s, Kashmir had become LeT's principal operational theatre. The organisation developed training and recruitment networks and directed fighters towards attacks on Indian security forces. Stephen Tankel, in, describes Kashmir as the group's primary objective even as its connections to the wider global jihadist movement expanded.This distinction is important. LeT developed relationships with al Qaida and other jihadist groups, but its core focus remained India and Kashmir. Riedel similarly distinguishes between the different objectives of the groups operating in the region, noting that the Afghan Taliban remained primarily focused on Afghanistan while LeT concentrated on South Asia. At the operational level, however, their cooperation increased.Saeed's prominence grew alongside the institutional development of MDI and LeT. He was not simply the leader of an armed organisation. The network around him combined religious propagation, education, charity and terror activity.Riedel describes Saeed as a prominent Pakistani Sunni scholar who worked with Azzam in developing MDI. The organisation's combination of religious activity and military infrastructure provided the foundation for the later growth of LeT.LeT's recruitment base was also closely connected to Pakistani society. Riedel writes that the organisation was predominantly Punjabi and recruited from many of the same communities and neighbourhoods as the Pakistani army and ISI. He also describes LeT camps located near army bases and the involvement of retired military personnel in training fighters.The nature and extent of state support for LeT has remained a matter of dispute, but the organisation's relationship with Pakistan's security establishment became an important part of its history. The United Nations Security Council identifies LeT as a Pakistan-based organisation and records its links with al Qaida and the Taliban, as well as its use of Jamaat-ud-Dawa for financial, logistical and infrastructural support.The September 11, 2001 attacks changed the environment for militant organisations operating from Pakistan. The United States designated LeT as a Foreign Terrorist Organisation in December 2001, while Pakistan banned the group in January 2002.The ban, however, did not eliminate the network. The US state department says Saeed subsequently changed the group's name to Jamaat-ud-Dawa and expanded its humanitarian activities, while continuing to disseminate its message through JuD's media outlets.Riedel similarly writes that although LeT was formally banned, it continued to operate and Saeed remained in charge. He describes the organisation's large facility at Muridke near Lahore, which included schools, dormitories, a garment factory, an iron foundry and a mosque.This structure helped the network maintain a presence beyond its armed operations. Religious institutions, charitable activity, fundraising and recruitment provided a broader organisational base that could continue even when the LeT name itself faced restrictions.The United Nations says LeT used JuD as a front through which it provided financial, logistical and infrastructural support for terrorist activity. It also records that an al Qaida operative, Abu Zubaydah, was captured in 2002 in a LeT safe house in Faisalabad, illustrating the organisation's connections to the wider jihadist network.The years after 2001 saw LeT's operational reach extend beyond the traditional Kashmir battlefield. The United Nations records that the organisation conducted terrorist operations against military and civilian targets from the 1990s onwards, including attacks in New Delhi and Mumbai and the December 2001 Parliament attack, in which Jaish-e-Mohammed was also involved.The 2008 Mumbai attacks represented the most significant expansion of that reach. Ten attackers carried out coordinated assaults across Mumbai between November 26 and 29, killing 166 people. The attack targeted several locations, including the Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel, the Oberoi-Trident and Nariman House.The operation also demonstrated the organisational depth behind LeT's attacks. Riedel's account details the role of David Coleman Headley, who joined LeT in Pakistan and later conducted reconnaissance in Mumbai. Between 2005 and 2008, Headley travelled repeatedly to India, studying targets, recording locations and reporting back to LeT.The Mumbai operation therefore represented more than an extension of the Kashmir insurgency. It demonstrated the organisation's ability to plan and execute a complex attack far from its traditional theatre while drawing on personnel, training and logistical networks developed over decades.The shift to Kashmir did not end LeT's involvement in Afghanistan. Instead, the two theatres became connected through overlapping militant networks.Riedel wrote that LeT became increasingly active in Afghanistan, including operations against Indian interests and clashes with Nato forces. He also described growing operational links between LeT and the Afghan Taliban, particularly the Haqqani network.The United Nations likewise records LeT's activity in Afghanistan and its links with al Qaida and the Taliban. The Australian government has documented LeT's continued presence in Afghanistan and reported that the UN estimated the group had close to 1,000 members operating there in May 2020.Afghanistan therefore remained an important part of LeT's network even after Kashmir became its main operational focus. The relationships, training environments and infrastructure developed during the Afghan jihad continued to provide connections to other militant organisations.Saeed's subsequent legal history illustrates the difference between Pakistan's formal action against LeT and the organisation's continued existence through associated structures.Pakistan arrested Saeed in 2019 on terrorism-financing charges. He was convicted in several cases and received additional sentences in subsequent proceedings. The UN Security Council's current sanctions information says Saeed is in Pakistani custody serving a cumulative 78-year sentence following convictions in seven terrorism-financing cases.India, meanwhile, has continued to pursue him over alleged involvement in major terror attacks attributed to LeT.The latest development is the NIA's supplementary chargesheet in the Pahalgam case. The agency has named Saeed both individually and as the chief of LeT and TRF, alleging that he was part of the wider conspiracy behind the April 2025 attack.The subsequent non-bailable warrant followed the NIA's request for Saeed's arrest and custodial interrogation. Meanwhile, Mumbai Police has begun the process for an in-absentia trial against Saeed and five other Pakistan-based accused in the 26/11 case.Lashkar-e-Taiba's four-decade history can be traced through a sequence of changing battlefields and organisational forms. Its foundations were laid during the Afghan jihad, when Hafiz Saeed and Abdullah Azzam helped build MDI and the networks around it. After the Soviet withdrawal, the organisation redirected much of its experience and infrastructure towards Kashmir, where it became a major Pakistan-based militant group.The 2002 ban did not erase the network. It adapted through Jamaat-ud-Dawa and other associated structures, while maintaining religious, charitable and recruitment networks across Pakistan. Its links with militant groups operating in Afghanistan also survived, even as India and Kashmir remained its central focus.The Mumbai attacks showed how far that network could project violence beyond Kashmir. The Pahalgam investigation has now brought the story back to the same region where LeT established much of its early operational identity.The latest legal proceedings against Saeed therefore sit at the end of a history that began not in Mumbai or Pahalgam, but in the Afghan jihad of the 1980s.
Article Summary: The legal case against Hafiz Muhammad Saeed has acquired a fresh dimension in India. The National Investigation Agency named Saeed in a supplementary chargesheet in the Pahalgam terror attack case. The development came as Mumbai Police separately began proceedings for a trial in absentia against Saeed and five other Pakistan-based accused in the 2008 Mumbai attacks.

Article Title: Pakistan hospital fire: 8 officials suspended over deaths of 14 newborns
Article Text: Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered the suspension of eight officials and directed that criminal proceedings be initiated against those found responsible for a fire that killed 14 newborns at a hospital in Islamabad, his office said on Saturday.Sharif issued the orders after an interim report by an investigative committee found serious lapses in fire safety and emergency preparedness at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS).The fire broke out on the third-floor nursery on Wednesday, where 15 newborns were being treated. The blaze spread rapidly, and hospital staff were able to rescue only one baby, officials said.The committee found that the nursery had neither a fire alarm nor a sprinkler system. It also said the hospital lacked detailed procedures and adequate training to deal with fires and other emergencies.The report said supervisory staff were not present when the fire broke out. Two nurses, a female security guard and a house officer were in the ward at the time.Emergency services were alerted six minutes after the fire started, while the first responders arrived 15 minutes after receiving the call, according to the interim report.Investigators also found that only two of the hospital's 13 standard operating procedures dealt with fires or other emergencies.“Those guilty of criminal negligence deserve no leniency,” Sharif was quoted as saying by the Associated Press. He ordered departmental and criminal proceedings against officials identified by the inquiry committee.Those facing action include the hospital's executive director, two joint executive directors, the head of the neonatal department, two doctors, the assistant director for security and the head of the Capital Development Authority's emergency services.Sharif also approved action against the private company responsible for hospital security and its officials.The government has announced compensation of 5 million Pakistani rupees (around $18,000) for each bereaved family.The interim report also recommended recognition for a nurse who risked her life to save a newborn before the flames spread through the ward. Sharif approved the recommendation to confer the Sitara-i-Khidmat, a state award for public service, on her.The deaths have triggered public anger and demands for accountability from grieving families and civil society groups.The incident has also prompted wider reviews of fire-safety arrangements at hospitals across Pakistan. Punjab authorities this week ordered an immediate assessment of fire-safety systems, firefighting equipment and emergency-response facilities at hospitals across the province.The fire was among Pakistan's deadliest recent tragedies involving children. In June, 14 schoolchildren were killed when the roof of an under-construction tutoring centre collapsed in Lahore.
Article Summary: Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered the suspension of eight officials. He has also directed that criminal proceedings be initiated against those found responsible for a fire that killed 14 newborns at a hospital in Islamabad. The fire broke out on the third-floor nursery on Wednesday, where 15 newborns were being treated.

Article Title: Pakistan: Three missing men found dead with alleged torture marks in Balochistan
Article Text:
Representative file photo (IANS photo)

Three bodies recovered in Balochistan's Usta Muhammad have reportedly been identified as men who had earlier gone missing, with local sources alleging that they were forcibly disappeared after being detained by Pakistani security forces.According to The Balochistan Post, the deceased have been identified as Hafiz Mohammad Waqas, a Levies personnel from Machh in Bolan, his brother Mittha Khan, son of Nawab Khan, and Maqbool Ahmed, son of Jan Mohammad, a resident of Dasht Sabzband.Waqas was reportedly taken into custody and forcibly disappeared in May 2026. The three bodies were recovered from Usta Muhammad on August 24, according to local sources cited by the publication.The sources said the bodies bore apparent signs of torture. However, the circumstances surrounding their deaths have not been independently established, and no official findings from an investigation have been made public.The recoveries come amid reports of more than 15 bodies being found in different parts of Balochistan in recent days, including Panjgur, Mastung and Kharan. Several bodies recovered from Panjgur were allegedly identified as people who had previously been reported missing, while the identities of others remain unknown.The latest cases have renewed scrutiny of allegations of enforced disappearances in Balochistan, where rights groups and political organisations have for years raised concerns over the fate of missing people.Baloch political and human rights organisations have accused Pakistani security institutions of detaining people and, in some cases, killing them in custody before abandoning their bodies. Pakistan's authorities and security institutions have repeatedly denied involvement in enforced disappearances and allegations of extrajudicial killings.Rights groups and political organisations have called for credible and transparent investigations into the reported disappearances and deaths. They have also demanded that missing individuals be produced before courts, their families be informed of their whereabouts, and anyone accused of wrongdoing be subjected to due legal process.
Article Summary: Three bodies recovered in Balochistan's Usta Muhammad have reportedly been identified as men who had earlier gone missing. Local sources allege they were forcibly disappeared after being detained by Pakistani security forces. The circumstances surrounding their deaths have not been independently established, and no official findings from an investigation have been made public.

Article Title: 15 newborns killed in fire at Islamabad hospital's gynaecology ward in Pakistan
Article Text:
The fire reportedly started after an air-conditioner compressor exploded inside the nursery, according to rescue sources.

Poll Vote & Share your view What should hospitals prioritise to prevent fire-related tragedies? Stronger fire-safety measures Regular safety inspections 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

15 newborns died after a fire broke out in the gynaecology ward of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) in Islamabad on Wednesday.According to PIMS officials, the nursery housed 16 newborns when the fire broke out, with only one baby rescued from the ward, reported local outlet Geo News. The fire reportedly started after an air-conditioner compressor exploded inside the nursery, according to rescue officials.The blaze broke out at around 7 am in the gynaecology ward of the hospital on the third floor of the MCH ward, in Pakistan's federal capital. Rescue teams were deployed to the hospital and worked to extinguish the fire and evacuate those inside while carrying out cooling operations at the site.According to the district administration, 14 of the 15 children killed were completely burnt.The incident has raised concerns over safety measures in the hospital's neonatal and maternity facilities.Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered an immediate investigation into the incident and directed authorities to identify those responsible and take strict action. He expressed deep grief over the deaths, saying that a tragedy involving children was an “irreparable loss”, and said he shared the grief of the bereaved parents.The Prime Minister also directed authorities to conduct a detailed review of fire-safety arrangements and the factors that contributed to the incident, with the aim of preventing similar tragedies in hospitals.Meanwhile, an inquiry committee headed by the additional deputy commissioner general has also been formed to determine how the fire started and establish responsibility. The blaze broke out in the hospital’s gynaecology ward, where the nursery was located.
Article Summary: 15 newborns died after a fire broke out in the gynaecology ward of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad. The fire reportedly started after an air-conditioner compressor exploded inside the nursery, according to rescue sources. Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered an immediate investigation into the incident.

Article Title: Five labourers gunned down at construction site in Pakistan's Balochistan
Article Text: Five labourers from Pakistan’s Punjab province were shot dead at a construction site in Balochistan’s Pishin district, a provincial government official said Tuesday, according to news agency PTI.The labourers were killed by unidentified gunmen in Saranan town on Monday morning, Balochistan government spokesperson Shahid Rind said. Their bodies were sent to their hometowns in Punjab for burial.Arrangements were made to transport the bodies to their respective villages in Ahmedpur Sharqia and Bahawalpur, Rind said. Security forces have launched a search operation to track down the attackers.Balochistan chief minister Sarfaraz Bugti condemned the killings and vowed action against those responsible."Those shedding the blood of innocent laborers deserve no leniency," Bugti said in a statement issued by his office. "The cowardly acts of terrorists cannot weaken the provincial government's resolve."Saranan town has witnessed militant attacks since last week. A few days ago, gunmen attacked a police station in the town and fled with weapons, ammunition and two vehicles.Banned Baloch insurgent groups have frequently targeted workers and labourers from other provinces working in Balochistan.In July, five barbers from Multan were shot dead in Mashkail town after armed men on motorcycles opened fire at their barber shop.Last month, six labourers from Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa were abducted in the Nasirabad area of Turbat district. Their bullet-riddled bodies were later found in a remote area, police said.Security and law enforcement agencies have been conducting a large-scale operation against insurgent groups in parts of Balochistan since early July. However, the attacks have continued.In a separate incident on Sunday, five policemen were injured when two unidentified men hurled a hand grenade at a police post in Ambar tehsil of Mohmand district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.Police retaliated with gunfire, forcing the attackers to flee. The injured policemen were taken to a nearby hospital and are said to be out of danger. An investigation is underway.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which borders Afghanistan, has witnessed recurring militant violence, including attacks linked to insurgent groups, cross-border movement of fighters and repeated military operations.
Article Summary: The labourers were killed by unidentified gunmen in Saranan town on Monday morning. Security forces have launched a search operation to track down the attackers. Baloch insurgent groups have frequently targeted workers and labourers from other provinces working in Balochistan. In July, five barbers from Multan were shot dead in Mashkail town.

Article Title: Pakistan army officer pulls gun, fires in air amid student protest at Peshawar university- video
Article Text:
Sarhad University, Peshawar, Pakistan (Picture from X)

A Pakistan army officer opened fire into the air during a student protest at Sarhad University in Peshawar, triggering chaos and a scuffle on the campus, according to local media reports and videos circulating online.The incident comes amid growing unrest in Pakistan, with protests and demonstrations also being reported from Pakistan-occupied Kashmir and Balochistan, adding to the challenges facing the country's military and political establishment.According to reports, the officer, said to be a colonel, was the husband of a faculty member at Sarhad University. He reportedly got into a heated confrontation with protesting students, which soon escalated into a physical scuffle.Videos shared by several social media accounts purportedly show the officer striking students with a stick amid the confrontation. As tensions escalated, he allegedly pulled out a pistol and initially pointed it towards the protesters before raising the weapon in the air.The officer was then seen firing shots into the air, sparking panic and further uproar on the university campus.Reports said the officer has been taken into custody, while the Pakistan army has ordered an inquiry into the incident.
Article Summary: Pakistan army officer opened fire during student protest at Sarhad University. Incident triggered chaos and a scuffle on the campus, according to reports. Incident comes amid growing unrest in Pakistan, with protests and demonstrations also being reported from Pakistan-occupied Kashmir and Balochistan.

Article Title: ‘CTA intentionally prevented’: PTI alleges negligence over Imran Khan’s hospital visit
Article Text:
Imran Khan’s medical care under scrutiny

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think the inquiry committee established by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif will lead to accountability? Yes, it will No, it won't 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), the party of former Prime Minister Imran Khan, on Monday criticised what it called the “continued failure” of authorities at a state-run hospital, alleging that a CT Coronary Angiography (CTA) scheduled for Khan was not conducted despite cardiologists warning of potential cardiac complications.In a statement on Sunday, PTI central secretary Information Sheikh Waqas Akram said authorities had failed to provide the 73-year-old Khan with the medically recommended diagnostic test despite a functional CT scanner being available at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS), Dawn reported."This cannot be dismissed as an isolated administrative lapse; it reflects a deeply troubling pattern,” Akram said.Akram also cited a Supreme Court order directing Khan to undergo a comprehensive medical examination and treatment at Shifa International Hospital.He alleged that authorities had bypassed the directive and instead transferred Khan to a facility where the CT angiography was not conducted.“When the necessary facilities were available at Shifa International, deliberately taking Khan to a hospital unable or unwilling to perform the procedure raises a grave question: was the decision made in advance to prevent the CT Coronary Angiography from being conducted?” he asked."Even the government’s own doctors considered this diagnostic test necessary,” Akram added.Akram said a government medical board examined Khan on August 10 after he complained of heart palpitations and severe headaches.He said a cardiologist at PIMS had recommended a CTA on August 1 after Khan experienced fluctuating blood pressure and restlessness, citing potential cardiac complications given his age and prolonged isolation.Taking note of the reports, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday formed an inquiry committee, headed by the Establishment Division secretary, to establish the facts and determine responsibility.Commenting on the Prime Minister’s decision to constitute an inquiry committee following reports that Imran Khan’s CTA was not conducted, Akram said the move raised “serious questions as to why the medically recommended test was not conducted in the first instance. Why coordination between the cardiology and radiology departments had failed, and why Imran Khan was not taken to Shifa International despite the availability of the required facilities there”."Imran Khan’s heart health cannot be subjected to political calculations, administrative excuses or further delay,” Akram said."Political victimisation must never be permitted to endanger a human life through the denial or postponement of essential medical care. The decision to take him to a facility where the required test was not conducted, despite the availability of the necessary facilities at Shifa International, has created serious concerns that the procedure was intentionally prevented,” he alleged."The government and all relevant authorities will bear full responsibility for any further deterioration in his condition,” Akram added.Meanwhile, former India captains Sunil Gavaskar, Kapil Dev and Dilip Vengsarkar are among 21 former international cricket captains who have written to Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, urging authorities to ensure proper medical treatment and the welfare of Imran Khan.The letter, initiated by former Australia captain Greg Chappell, marks the second appeal by former international cricketers calling for humane treatment and adequate medical care for the 73-year-old Khan.Khan was arrested on August 5, 2023, in connection with a corruption case and has remained in custody since then. He is currently lodged in Adiala Jail, a detention facility on the outskirts of Rawalpindi.Khan’s relatives and supporters have repeatedly alleged human rights violations and accused authorities of restricting his access to adequate medical care, family visits and legal counsel.
Article Summary: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), the party of former Prime Minister Imran Khan, on Monday criticised what it called the “continued failure” of authorities at a state-run hospital. PTI alleges that a CT Coronary Angiography (CTA) scheduled for Khan was not conducted despite cardiologists warning of potential cardiac complications. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday formed an inquiry committee, headed by the Establishment Division secretary.

Article Title: ‘You are powerful, but remember 1971?’ Pakistani politician takes fresh swipe at Army
Article Text:
Fazlur Rehman (File photo)

(With ANI inputs)

Pakistani politician and Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam (F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman continued his verbal attacks on the Pakistan Army, recalling the military's decisive defeat in the 1971 war with India that led to the creation of Bangladesh, then known as East Pakistan.“‘We are the protectors of this country. No one’s father can harm this country.’ I agree, you are very powerful,” Rehman remarked at a JUI (F) convention in Peshawar, targeting Pakistan’s top military leadership.He recalled how the Pakistan Army laid down its arms in 1971, just a day after then-President and military ruler General Yahya Khan declared that it would fight until the end."But I remember, and maybe there are some elders who remember, that in December 1971, one day before laying down arms, General Yahya Khan addressed the army and said, we will fight in the streets, in the deserts, in the fields, in the factories, in the mountains, and we will fight against them. We will fight. We heard these big words then," Rehman added.The JUI-F further chief questioned why the public is being subjected to "severe hardships" while the establishment remains "insensitive" to their misery.“Why are you putting the country and the people to the test? Why are you having fun when your public is suffering? And today is 2026. When the revolution came in Afghanistan in 1989, and the war started, now you tell me, it’s been 45-46 years, blood has been flowing on the same line for about half a century.When blood flows like this, then it is a sign of geographical changes,” Rehman remarked.Warning that persistent state oppression and ongoing conflict threaten the nation’s integrity and could signal territorial disintegration, he stated, “It is a sign of oppression. Then at least inform us of your intentions. We are tolerating it and will continue to tolerate it. It will continue. A few more days, my dear, just a few more days. We are forced to take a breath in the shade of oppression. If we endure the oppression for a little longer, if we suffer, if we cry, it is the legacy of our ancestors. We are helpless.”Rehman’s remarks came days after he challenged the military to enter politics directly, declaring, “If you want to do politics, then take off the uniform and come; participate in the elections, and it will become clear what votes people give to those in uniform. It is your prerogative to give government to whomever you want, and to snatch it away from whomever you wish.”
Article Summary: Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam (F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman continued his verbal attacks on the Pakistan Army. He recalled the military's decisive defeat in the 1971 war with India that led to the creation of Bangladesh. He questioned why the public is being subjected to "severe hardships" while the establishment remains "insensitive"

Article Title: Pakistan: Security official killed by unidentified gunmen; 5 cops injured in separate grenade blast
Article Text:
According to police, two unidentified armed men targeted the security official. (Photo credit: IANS)

Five policemen injured in grenade attack

A security official was killed on Sunday after unidentified gunmen opened fire in northwest Pakistan, police said, according to news agency PTI.The incident took place within the jurisdiction of Badaber Police Station on the outskirts of Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.According to police, two unidentified armed men riding a motorcycle targeted the official, who was posted with the Counter Terrorism Department.He was killed on the spot, while the assailants fled the scene following the attack. Police cordoned off the area and launched a search operation to trace the attackers.No individual or group has so far claimed responsibility for the attack.In a separate incident in Mohmand district, five policemen were injured when two unidentified men hurled a hand grenade at a police post in Ambar tehsil, police said.Police retaliated with gunfire, forcing the attackers to flee. The injured policemen were taken to a nearby hospital and are said to be out of danger. An investigation is underway.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which borders Afghanistan, has witnessed recurring militant violence, cross-border movement of fighters and military operations.Pakistan's federal government has blamed the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) for attacks in areas bordering Afghanistan since a ceasefire agreement between the two sides ended in November 2022.
Article Summary: A security official was killed on Sunday after unidentified gunmen opened fire in northwest Pakistan. In a separate incident, five policemen were injured when two unidentified men hurled a hand grenade at a police post in Ambar tehsil. The injured policemen were taken to a nearby hospital and are said to be out of danger.

Article Title: Pakistan power crisis: Karachi residents riot amid outages lasting hours, block major roads
Article Text:
Protesters blocked major roads and intersections, burned tyres and clashed with K-Electric personnel over prolonged blackouts (ANI photo)

Power protests erupted across several parts of Karachi as residents took to the streets over prolonged and unannounced outages, blocking major roads and burning tyres while demanding restoration of electricity.Demonstrations were reported in Pak Colony, Liaquatabad, Gharibabad, Nishtar Road, Bhimpura and Ranchore Line, disrupting traffic across key parts of Pakistan’s commercial capital. In Liaquatabad, protesters blocked major intersections, while clashes between traders and K-Electric (KE) staff over outages escalated into tyre-burning on Nishtar Road, as reported by local news outle Dawn.Residents said they were facing 12 hours or more of daily power cuts, often without adequate notice. The outages have also disrupted water supplies as pumping stations remain shut when electricity is unavailable, adding to public anger.“Bill-paying citizens are being punished with 12-hour load-shedding,” a protester in Liaquatabad said.The crisis also hit businesses and households, with residents reporting spoiled food, disrupted studies and sleepless nights as fans remained unusable during blackouts.The protests compounded an already severe traffic situation in the city. Roads were also closed for traditional Chup Tazia processions, while the power protests triggered additional blockades. Traffic police diverted vehicles to alternative routes, but those too became congested.Asif Khan, a private-sector employee, told Dawn he took four hours to travel from SITE to Liaquatabad after leaving work around 5pm. Another commuter said an ambulance carrying his feverish mother was stuck for about two hours near Civic Centre while they were travelling to a doctor in Saddar.“We pay bills on time but still face 12-hour power outages. Today we couldn’t even reach home,” commuter Imran from Gharibabad said.KE, however, attributed the prolonged outages in some affected areas to electricity theft and unpaid bills. A company spokesperson said outstanding dues from defaulters in Bandhani Colony and Rexer Line had crossed PKR 3 billion, adding that the duration of load-shedding depended on “electricity theft and the level of losses in the area”.The protests come as Karachi continues to grapple with an electricity crisis that is also affecting water supply, businesses and daily life across densely populated neighbourhoods.
Article Summary: Demonstrations reported in Pak Colony, Liaquatabad, Gharibabad, Nishtar Road, Bhimpura and Ranchore Line. Protesters blocked major roads and intersections, burned tyres and clashed with K-Electric personnel. Residents said they were facing 12 hours or more of daily power cuts, often without adequate notice.

Article Title: 'India could use water as weapon': Pakistan minister as Indus Waters Treaty remains in abeyance
Article Text:
Pakistan minister Ahsan Iqbal (File photo)

Pakistan minister Ahsan Iqbal has said India could “weaponise” the Indus Water Treaty (IWT) and expressed hope that “better sense” would prevail to prevent the two neighbours from going to war again, this time over water.He noted that the treaty had remained “untouchable” for almost seven decades since it was signed in 1960, but New Delhi has now been kept in abeyance “unilaterally."“...Indus Water Treaty that has stood the test of time for the last 70 years. India and Pakistan fought several wars, but it (IWT) was considered untouchable because it is an international agreement, and this time around the Indian government has unilaterally held it in abeyance... first time probably water has been weaponised in history,” Iqbal told the Asia Society.“We (Pakistan) now face this threat that they (India) can use water as a weapon to deny Pakistan when it needs it for its crops and release it when we don't need it... We are using all the diplomatic means to make sure that we don't have future wars on water because we have already seen lots of wars,” the minister added.He further stated that South Asian countries should instead focus on issues such as development, poverty, illiteracy and the youth “bulge”, describing the region as the “least integrated” in the world."So we hope that there is better sense in our neighbour's (India) mind and we don't see that water is weaponised and we go to another conflict with India over water because Pakistan cannot surrender at any cost the future of its 250 million people for its food security and right of water. If we let it happen, then every state that is on the lower side of water supply would be hostage to any country that controls the rivers," the Pakistan Muslim League (Nawaz) leader remarked.Iqbal's remarks came days after Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif warned India of a “direct response” for putting the IWT in abeyance.“India proved itself an enemy of peace by unilaterally and illegally suspending the Indus Waters Treaty. I declare in clear terms that every single drop of Pakistan's water is our red line. If India does not come to its senses, it will be responded to directly,” Sharif said on August 13, on the eve of Pakistan's Independence Day.New Delhi put the agreement in abeyance following the Pahalgam terror attack in April last year. Since then, Pakistani leaders have repeatedly called water their “red line” and threatened India over the move, describing it as an “act of war.”
Article Summary: Ahsan Iqbal says India could use water as a weapon to deny Pakistan when it needs it for its crops. New Delhi put the agreement in abeyance following the Pahalgam terror attack in April last year. Pakistani leaders have repeatedly called water their “red line” and threatened India.

Article Title: ‘In contempt for gathering people’: Pak blames ex PM Imran Khan’s party for hospital transfer
Article Text:
Pakistan government statement on Imran Khan's hospital transfer

Poll Vote & Share your view How do you view the involvement of PTI workers during Imran Khan transfer to the hospital? Justified, they were supporting their leader Unsure 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Govt says court order was followed

NEW DELHI: The Pakistan government on Saturday blamed jailed former prime minister Imran Khan ’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party for his transfer to a state-run hospital instead of the private facility ordered by the Supreme Court for his medical checkup.Information minister Attaullah Tarar said the government was forced to take 73-year-old Khan to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) after a large number of PTI workers gathered outside Shifa International Hospital.The development came after Khan’s sister, Uzma Khan, approached the Supreme Court alleging that the government and senior officials had violated its order to shift the former prime minister to the private hospital.The Supreme Court had on August 18 directed authorities to transfer Khan from Adiala jail to Shifa Hospital within two days and keep him there until the next hearing on September 16. Instead, Khan was taken to PIMS and later returned to jail after doctors declared him fit.Tarar alleged that PTI workers gathered along the route to Shifa Hospital, removed barriers and created social media content, leaving authorities with no option but to shift Khan elsewhere.“Contempt has definitely happened,” Tarar said, accusing Khan’s sister and PTI of violating the court’s directions by turning the medical checkup into a political issue.The minister maintained that the government had implemented the Supreme Court’s order “in letter and spirit”. He said the medical examination was conducted transparently, Khan’s sister was present and doctors from Shifa Hospital were involved in the process.The Supreme Court’s order followed months of concerns raised by Khan’s family and supporters over his health, particularly an eye condition diagnosed earlier this year. Khan was taken to PIMS several times after being diagnosed with right central retinal vein occlusion in late January.A report submitted by jail authorities to the Supreme Court said his eye condition had improved significantly and that his vision was “almost normal”.Khan has been lodged in Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail since 2023 in connection with several cases.
Article Summary: Pakistan government blames jailed former prime minister Imran Khan ’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party for his transfer to a state-run hospital. Information minister Attaullah Tarar said the government was forced to take 73-year-old Khan to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences. Tarar alleged that PTI workers gathered along the route to Shifa Hospital, removed barriers and created social media content.

Article Title: Big crisis brewing in Rawalpindi? Pakistan deploys army for ‘sensitive duties’
Article Text:
The decision comes days after a man allegedly linked to former prime minister Imran Khan's party.

Army deployment follows security incident

Rawalpindi has strategic importance

The Pakistan government has authorised the deployment of the army in Rawalpindi for six months following a request from the Punjab home department for what it described as "sensitive security duties".The decision allows three companies of the Pakistan Army to be deployed in the city under Article 245 of the Pakistani Constitution, which permits the armed forces to assist the civil administration in maintaining security."The federal government, exercising the powers conferred under Article 245 of the Constitution of Pakistan, is pleased to authorise the deployment of three companies of the Pakistan Army for sensitive security duties in Rawalpindi," according to a notification issued by the Ministry of Interior and Narcotics Control on Friday.The notification said the deployment was intended to prevent a potential security problem and ensure that authorities could respond quickly if an unexpected situation arose.It said that the decision was taken "to avoid any undesirable situation as well as to respond effectively in any unforeseen situation as per the requirement of the district administration".The decision comes days after a man allegedly linked to former prime minister Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party opened fire at security forces in Rawalpindi.He was subsequently killed in retaliatory firing.State-run PTV News, citing security sources, reported that the attacker was a resident of Khyber district and an "active PTI member". According to the report, a PTI flag, bullets and weapons were recovered from him.The PTI, however, rejected any connection with the incident. The party said it had nothing to do with terrorism and accused authorities of attempting to associate the party with the attack.The deployment is particularly significant because Rawalpindi is home to the Pakistan Army's General Headquarters, the military's top command centre.The city is therefore an important military and administrative centre, and the decision to deploy army personnel there comes amid heightened security concerns following the recent shooting incident.The deployment has been authorised for six months, with the troops to perform duties requested by the district administration under the constitutional provision allowing the military to assist civilian authorities.
Article Summary: Three companies of the Pakistan Army will be deployed in Rawalpindi for six months. The decision comes after a man allegedly linked to Imran Khan's party opened fire in the city. The deployment is intended to prevent a potential security problem and ensure that authorities can respond quickly.

Article Title: 'Repeatedly tortured': Imran Khan's sister alleges abuse in jail as ex-Pakistan PM returns to prison
Article Text:
‘He was repeatedly tortured in jail’: Imran Khan's sister alleges mistreatment

PTI files contempt petition

Supporters gather after brief hospital visit

Pakistan's jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan repeatedly told his sister that he was being tortured in prison, she said on Saturday, a day after he was taken to a state-run hospital for a brief medical examination and sent back to jail.Khan's sister, Uzma Khan, attended his examination at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) in Islamabad and said the former prime minister was physically fit but had repeatedly complained of torture.“Khan told me that he is being repeatedly tortured in prison”, she told the media.The interior and law ministries, along with jail authorities, have not responded to a Reuters request for comment on the allegation.Khan was taken to PIMS overnight on Friday after the Supreme Court had directed authorities to transfer him from Adiala jail to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad for a medical examination. He was declared medically fit and returned to prison within hours.Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party on Saturday filed a contempt petition against the government, accusing authorities of violating the Supreme Court's order by taking him to PIMS instead of the private hospital named by the court.The petition seeks action against senior government officials and asks that Khan be taken to Shifa International Hospital for treatment, PTI legal adviser Naeem Panjutha said."The petition seeks action against the ​prime minister, law minister, information minister" and other government officials, Panjutha said, adding that it also calls for Khan's treatment at the private hospital ordered by the court.The PTI also alleged that Khan was denied access to his personal physician, which it said amounted to another breach of the Supreme Court's directive.A three-judge Supreme Court bench had on Tuesday directed authorities to transfer Khan from Adiala jail to Shifa International Hospital within two days for a medical examination.The PTI interprets the order as requiring Khan to remain under medical supervision until at least mid-September.Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said the decision to take Khan to PIMS instead of the court-named private hospital was made because of security concerns.Khan declared medically fit, sent back to jailKhan was examined by a team of doctors, including an ophthalmologist, cardiologist and physician, before being declared medically fit and sent back to Adiala jail in Rawalpindi."A team of qualified doctors, including an ophthalmologist, a cardiologist and a physician conducted a detailed examination of him and declared him medically fit," Tarar said.Khan has been imprisoned since August 2023 and maintains that the cases against him are politically motivated. The government denies the allegation.His lawyers have previously said his health has deteriorated in prison and that he has suffered substantial loss of vision in his right eye. The government has maintained that medical reports have found no condition requiring immediate treatment.Khan's supporters gathered along roads in Islamabad overnight, throwing flowers at a vehicle believed to be carrying him to the hospital.The scenes were broadcast live on Pakistani television, in a notable departure from recent years when broadcasters often avoided mentioning Khan's name.PTI leaders have warned that the latest developments could increase pressure on the government and fuel fresh demonstrations."After what happened yesterday, the pressure (on authorities) will double," Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi said, adding that preparations for a protest march planned for September 27 had picked up.Khan's arrest and imprisonment have remained a major source of political tension in Pakistan. His arrest in 2023 triggered widespread protests, including attacks on military installations, and his supporters continue to demand his release.
Article Summary: Imran Khan repeatedly told his sister that he was being tortured in prison, she says. Khan was taken to a state-run hospital for a brief medical examination and sent back to jail.
