He was declared medically fit and returned to prison within hours. Khan has been imprisoned since August 2023 and maintains that the cases against him are politically motivated.

Article Title: Nepal flash floods: Death toll rises to 903, over 4,200 still missing as rescue operations intensify
Article Text:
Death toll reaches 903 in Nepal flash floods

Rescue teams deployed across affected areas

The death toll from catastrophic flash floods and landslides in Nepal has risen to 903, according to Nepalese authorities, as large-scale rescue operations continue across flood-hit areas.The disaster has also left around 4,247 people missing, while 10,451 people have been rescued so far, the data showed.The floods and landslides, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche along the Tibet border, have left thousands of people missing or uncontactable, while nearly 20,000 security personnel and 14 military helicopters have been deployed for rescue and relief operations.The government of Andhra Pradesh said that, as of 7 am on Monday, an estimated 2,500 to 3,000 people remained missing or uncontactable, while more than 8,700 people had been evacuated by security forces.Several Indian nationals are also still untraceable following the floods and landslides. Authorities said between 149 and 180 Indians have been evacuated, while around 275 to 320 remain missing or uncontactable.Among those unaccounted for are 14 pilgrims from Andhra Pradesh, including seven from the state and seven non-resident Indians.Meanwhile, 20 Telugu pilgrims who survived the floods safely reached Kathmandu from Tibet.The Andhra Pradesh government said a group of 144 pilgrims arrived in Kathmandu from Saga County, Tibet, through the Kodari checkpoint at around 11 pm on Sunday.The group includes 20 Telugu pilgrims, including Sastry and three members of his family. They are scheduled to travel to Mumbai on Tuesday before proceeding to their respective homes.Authorities are maintaining continuous coordination with Nepalese counterparts to locate and rescue stranded Indians, particularly pilgrims from Andhra Pradesh.Around 20,000 security personnel and 14 military helicopters remain engaged in relief operations, while six specialised surgical teams have been deployed to provide emergency medical assistance.India's specialised tunnel-rescue teams and technical experts are also assisting with operations at the Trishuli-3A hydropower tunnel, where workers remain trapped.More than 25 miles of roads and 40 suspension bridges have reportedly been destroyed, according to the Andhra Pradesh government.Heavy rainfall, landslides and blocked valleys continue to hamper rescue efforts. Authorities are also monitoring a potentially dangerous temporary lake formed in Tibet following severe flooding, amid concerns over further risks to affected areas.The Andhra Pradesh government said it remains in constant contact with Nepalese authorities regarding the evacuation, identification and welfare of Indian nationals, particularly pilgrims from the state.
Article Summary: Floods and landslides triggered by an ice-rock avalanche along the Tibet border. Thousands of people missing or uncontactable, while nearly 20,000 security personnel and 14 military helicopters deployed for rescue and relief operations. 20 Telugu pilgrims who survived the floods safely reached Kathmandu from Tibet.

Article Title: Nepal survivors return to ruins to salvage memories
Article Text:
File Photo: A man salvages a money and bottles of mineral water from his house affected by flash floods in Dhading District, Nepal

Days after a wall of water and debris ripped through Nepal, Shanti Lamichhane sat on a fruit crate in the dirt where her village once stood, staring at what remained of her home. Across Nepal’s flood disaster zone, survivors are returning to villages reduced to mud and debris, searching for belongings, documents and fragments of lives swept away in minutes.Lamichhane said she was waiting for bulldozers to finish clearing the path so she could return. “I want to retrieve a few things, but it is not just about that,” she told AFP. “All my memories are there too.”The village of Dhunge, once home to roughly 150 families, now lies in ruins, reduced to a swampy expanse with an ominous rotting stench — one of dozens of settlements obliterated by the floods. Forced to flee for their lives without time to take anything with them, many survivors are now returning to salvage whatever might remain — or simply to see what became of what they once called home.Hari Prasad Rimal returned to his home in the village of Devighat, hoping to recover treasured belongings. He brought back a photograph of his daughter. “It was pasted on a chest that was floating,” said Rimal, 44. “There was nothing else I could retrieve...” Rimal’s warehouse busine­ss, a few kilometres upstream, remained inaccessible, he said. Drone images showed only mud and debris where it had stood.In Dhunge, Navraj Upretti waded through knee-high sludge towards his home, flanked by two rescuers. “I have some imp­o­­rtant documents I really need,” he implored. Upretti, 40, said he had less than a minute to escape when the floods st­ru­ck. “The house was inundated; I managed to get barely 100 metres away,” said Upretti, who ran a restaurant in the area. All has been completely destroyed.
Article Summary: Survivors are returning to villages reduced to mud and debris, searching for belongings, documents and fragments of lives swept away in minutes. The village of Dhunge, once home to roughly 150 families, now lies in ruins, reduced to a swampy expanse with an ominous rotting stench.

Article Title: Hunt intensifies for 900 missing at hydel units, one tunnel head located
Article Text:
File Photo: A Nepal army official during a rescue operation for the people trapped inside the tunnel of the Upper Trishuli 3 'A' Hydropower Project in Nuwakot, Nepal

MEA cautions against relying on changing casualty figures

NUWAKOT (NEPAL)/DEHRADUN: Time running out for over 900 people missing from Nepal's flood-hit hydropower projects, rescue teams led by Nepalese Army personnel intensified operations to hunt for survivors, particularly at the Upper Trishuli-3A, where they located the tunnel's crown head and began widening an opening to send rescuers inside with oxygen cylinders.While the Independent Power Producers' Association Nepal said 537 workers and staff were unaccounted for across nine projects, Nepal's disaster management authority, NDRRMA, stated that 933 workers from hydropower projects were untraced.The number of dead rose to 810 Sunday - 794 in Nepal and 16 reported in Tibet - with 3,048 missing across both countries, as search ops entered a fifth day. NDRRMA listed 2,502 people missing and Tibet another 546. Nepal said 592 foreign nationals were among those missing, besides 127 Nepalese citizens travelling with foreign groups.MEA said at 5.30pm Sunday that 149 Indian nationals had been rescued in Nepal. Its latest missing-person tally, issued Saturday night, listed 275 Indian nationals missing and another 128 people of Indian origin as uncontactable. India had also not announced a confirmed number of Indian deaths by Sunday evening.Efforts to hunt for survivors at the nine hydropower projects picked up as weather improved slightly. Road access to Upper Trishuli-3A remained cut off, forcing Nepalese Army to airlift excavators, bulldozers and other earth-moving machinery to the project area using helicopters. Joint teams operated the machines through the night despite rain and moved closer to the tunnel entry point.Nepalese Army spokesperson Brig Gen Rajaram Basnet told TOI that the team, which included tunnel experts, had located the crown head - the main section - of Trishuli 3A. "A hole of 2x3ft was dug, which revealed a water surface spanning a diameter of around seven metres and extending to a significant height. An army expert entered the hole and looked for signs of life but with no luck so far," Basnet said."We're now trying to widen the hole area to allow more experts to enter with oxygen cylinders and search for those trapped," he added. By Sunday evening, around 8,500 Army personnel had been deployed across major flood-affected areas for search-and-rescue operations.At Upper Trishuli-1, around 300 workers were believed to have been trapped inside the tunnel, of whom 254 had been rescued, while search operations continued for the remaining workers. At Upper Trishuli-3B, 91 of the 122 workers earlier reported missing had been rescued and 31 remained unaccounted for, showing how the rescue effort had expanded far beyond the 100-odd workers initially feared trapped at a handful of sites.Nearly 20,000 security personnel had been deployed, while ground and aerial teams continued searches along riverbanks, destroyed settlements and mud-filled tunnels. Nepal foreign secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai said, “Our immediate national priority remains clear: to save lives, locate missing persons, rescue them, provide urgent relief to survivors, and ensure that affected Nepalese as well as foreign nationals receive appropriate assistance and support. ”As number of the dead and missing kept changing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal cautioned: “We are in a dynamic situation, so figures keep going up and down. Also, we have to reconcile several lists that we are dealing with.”Among the lists of “foreign nationals”, the count of people of Indian origin is likely to be high. Many travellers formally counted as American, British, Australian, Canadian and other nationals were people of Indian origin travelling on foreign passports, several of them on or returning from Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage.In one 77-member group caught in the disaster, 53 were people of Indian origin carrying foreign passports.The Indian picture on the Tibet side was also being counted separately. Chinese authorities said 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries were among the 546 missing in Gyirong, including 49 Indians, 104 Nepalese, 33 Latvians, 18 Americans, 15 Britons, six Canadians and six Australians.It remained unclear whether the 49 Indians listed in Tibet were already part of MEA’s broader count of 275 missing Indian citizens.Large numbers of Indian pilgrims and travellers stranded on the China side had meanwhile begun moving out. MEA said earlier Sunday that 598 Indians had crossed safely from China into Nepal over two days, while around 900 Indians who remained on the Chinese side were “safe and contactable”. Indian missions in Beijing and Kathmandu remained in touch with Chinese and Nepalese authorities.India intensified its technical assistance. Four relief flights had carried 68.5 tonnes of supplies to Kathmandu, while a 13-member Indian Army tunnel-rescue team with specialist equipment and six forensic teams comprising 19 personnel were sent to assist Nepalese authorities. Sixteen trucks carrying equipment for a 230-foot single-lane modular steel bridge had reached Nepal and equipment for seven more Bailey bridges was being supplied.
Article Summary: Number of dead rises to 810 Sunday - 794 in Nepal and 16 in Tibet - with 3,048 missing across both countries. Nepal said 592 foreign nationals were among those missing, besides 127 Nepalese citizens travelling with foreign groups. India had also not announced a confirmed number of Indian deaths.

Article Title: Bangladesh says no risk in joining Mecca defence pact with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkiye
Article Text:
"Hope to respond positively": Bangladesh signals interest in joining Mecca Defence Pact

Dhaka says pact will not restrict other alliances

Experts warn of possible foreign policy complications

Bangladesh on Sunday said it sees no risk in joining the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye, arguing that participation in the pact would not limit its engagement with other international partners, news agency PTI reported.State minister for foreign affairs Humaiun Kobir said Dhaka was holding discussions on the issue and that the talks were “progressing positively” with its bilateral partners. He said Bangladesh would pursue a flexible foreign policy while balancing its international relationships.“This is a unique pact that presents new opportunities,” Kobir told reporters after a meeting with Saudi Ambassador to Bangladesh Abdullah Zafer bin Abiyah.Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement on August 7 amid heightened security concerns in West Asia. The pact establishes a framework for collective deterrence and states that an armed attack against any one of the three signatories would be regarded as an attack against all.India has said it is closely monitoring developments related to the pact and will take necessary steps to safeguard its security interests.Kobir said joining one area of security cooperation would not prevent Bangladesh from contributing to other alliances or partnerships. He added that during his recent visit to Jeddah, he discussed the pact with several officials, including Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud, and received a “very positive” response.Foreign minister Khalilur Rahman had earlier told Parliament that Bangladesh viewed the pact positively and would consider joining if it received an invitation. However, he said Dhaka had not yet received any formal offer to join the agreement.Bangladeshi foreign policy experts and former diplomats have expressed reservations about Dhaka joining the military pact, saying it could mark a departure from the country's longstanding policy of non-alignment and potentially complicate ties with India.Former ambassador Mahfuzur Rahman said the pact may be important for Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye but was not essential for Bangladesh, which faces little likelihood of being drawn into the kinds of conflicts involving the existing members.Another former diplomat, Humayun Kabir, said Bangladesh would need to assess whether the security interests of the pact's members align with its own national, economic and strategic interests.
Article Summary: Bangladesh says it sees no risk in joining the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye. State minister for foreign affairs Humaiun Kobir said Dhaka was holding discussions on the issue and that the talks were “progressing positively”

Article Title: Nepal begins burials after preserving DNA; only 29 flood victims identified so far
Article Text:
An update issued said only 29 of the 650-plus bodies had been identified.

NUWAKOT, NEPAL: Authorities in Nepal began temporarily burying unidentified victims of Bhote Koshi-Trishuli-Naryani flood in shallow graves after collecting DNA and forensic evidence as morgues overflowed and remains recovered far downstream became increasingly difficult to identify.An update issued on Sunday evening said only 29 of the 650-plus bodies had been identified even as recoveries continued along the roughly 200km river system.Nepal Police spokesperson DIG Abi Narayan Kafle told TOI that 211 of the first 669 recovered remains were mutilated, partial or severed. “Many remains were buried under thick mud and water for two to three days,” he said. Bodies swept dozens of km from Rasuwa were recovered in Nuwakot, Chitwan, Gorkha, Tanahun and Nawalparasi, often far from where victims disappeared.Chitwan became the biggest pressure point. By Sunday, 259 bodies had been recovered along Trishuli and Narayani riverbanks there but only nine identified. Authorities began moving unidentified remains to Devghat forest after post-mortem examination and DNA collection, with 26 placed underground in the first batch.The process was designed so burial does not end a family’s search for closure -- every body was assigned an identification number; photographs, physical features, clothes, jewellery and other belongings were recorded, while DNA, fingerprints and other forensic samples were preserved.Burial locations were geo-tagged so remains could later be located and exhumed if relatives established identity.“If family members come forward in the future to claim a missing relative, these scientific and legal records will allow us to confirm identity and locate the exact burial plot,” Kafle said.Gorkha district also buried 29 unidentified bodies and body parts after collecting DNA. “Gorkha does not have sufficient mortuary facilities, and bodies are being recovered every day,” chief district officer Tulsi Prasad Shrestha said. Nawalparasi East began a similar process on Sunday, placing 20 unidentified remains underground after forensic sampling and assigning identification numbers.For families, identification increasingly depended on small personal details. More than 1,000 relatives reached Pokhara on Saturday to examine photographs of 102 bodies brought from downstream districts. Police said families recognised loved ones through tattoos, necklaces, earrings and even school uniforms.One father from Bidur identified his five-year-old son, whose body had been recovered far downstream in Nawalparasi, after seeing a photograph online. The clues were the child’s school tie, necklace and earring.“Where faces are no longer recognisable, relatives are identifying bodies through other things on their person,” police inspector Deepak Rijal said. “More relatives are continuing to arrive.”
Article Summary: Only 29 of the 650-plus bodies identified. 211 of the first 669 recovered remains were mutilated, partial or severed. Bodies swept dozens of km from Rasuwa were recovered in Nuwakot, Chitwan, Gorkha, Tanahun and Nawalparasi.

Article Title: Nepal floods: Stranger ran past school screaming ‘Run, water’. It saved 370 kids, teachers
Article Text:
Uttargaya Public English Secondary School (facebook image)

Poll Vote & Share your view How important do you think real-time communication is during emergencies? Extremely important Not very important 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NUWAKOT: “The big flood is coming, run...” An unidentified man sprinting past Uttargaya Public School in Betrawati, across the river and a few km from Trishuli Bazaar, shouting those words gave more than 370 pupils and their teachers the warning they desperately needed.Within minutes, children were scrambling towards the forested hill behind the campus as the surge cut across roads and normal escape routes. The school routine had barely begun on Wednesday. Hostel students were at breakfast when the cry rang through the compound. There had been no siren, automated message or official alert before the children began running.The warning that reached Uttargaya came from a stranger outside the compound — shouting loudly enough, and early enough for teachers to act. Older pupils from Grades 7 to 10 ran themselves; staff helped younger children through mud, carrying some in their arms when they could not keep up.“No one could have imagined a flood this massive was coming,” English teacher Somlal Dangol told TOI. “That’s why they didn't run far at first — and by the time they saw it, they could no longer escape along the main paths.”Grade 10 student Sujal Lama had finished his morning tuition and was heading towards the school's breakfast when the warning spread.He initially thought the river would not rise very high. “If I had gone to eat, the flood would have caught me,” Sujal told TOI on Sunday. He ran towards the forest, spent the night there and was given food by teachers once he had gathered enough courage -- his teachers said 'bravado' -- to return towards the building.Class 8 student Rashmi Tamang recalled the struggle uphill. “We managed to climb up even though we were covered in mud, but many children couldn't even run,” she told TOI.For one family, a parent’s attempt to reach the school ended in tragedy. Nawaraj Tamang rushed towards Uttargaya after learning about the flood to find his Grade 10 son Ayush. Before leaving, he told his mother, Mungsi Tamang, “Aama, ma Ayush lai lina aaye” (Mother, I have come to get Ayush). Nawaraj was swept away before he could reach the school. Ayush escaped into the forest and survived.In the immediate aftermath, vice-principal Pawan Sharma and teachers were scattered with groups of children on higher ground, communications disrupted and school records inaccessible.“Relatives of students are calling continuously from inside the country and abroad, but I don’t even have the records of those children with me anymore,” Sharma told TOI. “We have managed to hand over about 25 to 30% directly to their parents, and we have been in touch with the parents of others.”The school was still trying to trace many pupils after the flood, with disrupted communications making it difficult to establish how many had reached their families. No confirmed figure for student deaths from Uttargaya Public School had been released.
Article Summary: More than 370 pupils at Uttargaya Public School in Betrawati were affected by the flood. A stranger shouting 'The big flood is coming, run' gave pupils and their teachers the warning they desperately needed. The school was still trying to trace many pupils after the flood, with disrupted communications making it difficult to establish how many had reached their families.

Article Title: 'River rises, we run uphill; it falls, we return — then Trishuli sends us fleeing again'
Article Text:
People gathered after being evacuated, and the rescue operation was temporarily suspended as heavy rainfall worsened weather conditions, in Trishuli on Saturday. (ANI Video Grab)

TOI

TOI

TOI

Barrier lake has drained naturally, easing fresh flood threat: China

Poll Vote & Share your view How are residents coping with the frequent surges of the Trishuli River? Staying constantly alert and prepared to evacuate Feeling overwhelmed and anxious 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

TRISHULI BAZAAR: Nobody in Trishuli Bazaar -- and the cut-off Rasuwa district upstream -- unwinds anymore. A bag with critical documents, some dry food and a bottle of water remains close to the door. Shoes stay on. Phones remain fully charged and clutched tightly in hands even as one "sleeps". When Trishuli rises, people scamper uphill. When it falls, they tread back cautiously to what remains of their homes and businesses. Then another warning arrives from upstream and the climb starts again.Your correspondent watched that cycle repeat through Saturday night and Sunday morning.Around 3.30am Sunday, word began spreading that Bhote Koshi had risen sharply upstream. Phones started buzzing. Police and local authorities warned people in downstream areas to stay away from the river and move towards safer ground. Sleep disappeared.Shops and structures that once stood closest to Trishuli in the bazaar are already gone. Every fresh rise in the water now looks like the beginning of another disaster.“It's not possible to sleep,” Dawa Tamang, 42, proprietor of a garment store, told. He had moved uphill four times since the previous morning.“The river surged nearly three metres, swallowed our lower terrace, and then pulled back. Just as we started sweeping the silt away, word came of another surge upstream. We ran again.”The fresh water moved downstream through the morning. At one stage Trishuli was around three metres above danger level in parts of Dhading before the surge gradually weakened farther south. By the time it reached Narayani, officials said it had dropped below danger level.That offered relief on paper. Here, it did not feel like relief.A falling river now only means that people can descend for a few hours. They inspect damage, move belongings, wash away fresh layers of silt and try to eat. But they remain ready to leave again.“Every time a phone vibrates with a group text, your heart stops,” high school science teacher Bina Gurung, 28, said. “The kids are exhausted, the elders are anxious, and none of us dare to take off our jackets before dawn.”Night amplifies everything. Power has flickered. The valley turns completely dark. Trishuli cannot always be seen, but it can be heard below — a constant roar that people now listen to for changes.“The fear is psychological as much as it is physical,” relief worker Ramesh Adhikari, 34, told. “Everyone is sleeping in their boots, clutching their phones, listening to the sound of rain or for police sirens or neighbours shouting.”Rescue personnel, govt officials, aid workers and journalists have filled surviving lodges, guesthouses and homestays. Rooms on higher ground got sold-out first. Local families have opened spare bedrooms, living rooms and attics.Such is the load on hotels and homestays that Nepal's physical infrastructure minister Sunil Lamsal came to Trishuli Bazaar by a chopper, but had to return to Kathmandu hours later because he could not find accommodation. Along with home minister Sudhan Gurung, Lamsal is the closest aide to PM Balendra Shah.“In 30 years of running this inn, I have never seen anything like it,” River View owner Sarita Shrestha, 51, told. She had turned her family’s attic into sleeping space. “People are sleeping four to a bed, but even those staying lower down spend the whole night asking to be moved uphill.”A barrier lake formed near Nepal-China border after the massive ice-rock avalanche had almost completely drained through natural outflow by Sunday, easing fears of another sudden flood downstream, China’s ministry of water resources said. The lake formed near the confluence of Nepal’s Chhochen Khola and China’s Purepu Tsangpo after the glacier collapse on the northern face of Langtang Ri triggered the Bhote Koshi flood.Chinese hydrological teams estimated that around 2 million cubic metres of water had accumulated behind the natural blockage. Officials said water was now flowing normally through natural channels and most of the impounded water had been discharged without engineering intervention. Nepalese scientist Nitesh Khadka, who works at Chinese Academy of Sciences in Chengdu, shared photographs indicating that the lower barrier lake had drained. He said more than half the water in an upper lake had also flowed out.
Article Summary: People in Trishuli Bazaar are staying in their boots, clutching their phones, listening to the sound of rain or for police sirens or neighbours shouting. A bag with critical documents, some dry food and a bottle of water remains close to the door. Phones remain fully charged and clutched tightly in hands even as one "sleeps"
